retrieved_docs: [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] In brief Ding et al. mapped a single-cell projectome of 785 spinal projection neurons and 1,464 central relay neurons in thalamus, hypothalamus, PB, SCm, PAG, and medulla. They have constructed a high-resolution wiring diagram for the ascending somatosensory pathways based on projectome-defined subtypes. Highlights A brain-wide projectome of individual SPNs and central relay neurons - Revealed parallel, divergent, and convergent projection patterns Thalamic neurons send layer-specific projection to the cortex - Constructed a wiring diagram for ascending somatosensory pathways

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] SUMMARY Relay of multimodal somatosensory information from the spinal cord to the brain is critical for sensory perception, but the underlying circuit organization remains unclear. We have reconstructed mouse cervical spinal projection neurons at single-cell resolution and identified 19 projectome-defined subtypes exhibiting diverse projection patterns. We also reconstructed the brain-wide axonal projections of central relay neurons that receive direct spinal inputs at the single-cell resolution. We discovered parallel, divergent, and convergent projection patterns for spinal projection neurons and central relay neurons. Our results revealed the diverse pathways channeling spinal information to the cortex. Furthermore, we identified parallel lateral and medial spinal-superior colliculus-brainstem pathways, which could be involved in orienting and defensive behaviors, respectively. These data allowed us to construct a wiring diagram for ascending somatosensory pathways with projectome-defined subtype resolution. Our single-cell projectome analysis provided a new framework for understanding the complex neural circuitry underlying coordinated processing of diverse somatosensory modalities.

After 7 weeks, we acquired high-resolution images of the brain and cervical spinal cord using the fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography (fMOST) method $^{24,25}$ (Figures 1B, 1C, and S2A). Subsequently, we reconstructed the complete arborization of SPNs (785 neurons from 53 mice) using the semi-automatic tracing algorithm "fast neurite tracer" (FNT, see STAR Methods) $^{26}$ (Figures 1D and S2B-S2E) and registered these neurons to the Allen Common Coordinate Framework version 3 (CCFv3) $^{27,28}$ and to a cervical spinal cord template constructed in this study (Figures S2F-S2I). Despite an unexpected low number of labeled neurons in laminae 1/2 (L1/2) and laminar 3 (L3), the soma of reconstructed SPNs were widely distributed in laminar 4 (L4), L5/6, medial white matter (MWM), and LWM of the dorsal spinal cord (Figures S3A and S3B). Moreover, axons of reconstructed SPNs covered major brain areas targeted by bulk labeling, indicating extensive SPN subtype coverage (Figures S3C-S3E). SPNs project widely in the hypothalamus, thalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] INTRODUCTION The somatosensory system plays critical roles in processing diverse sensory signals that encode mechanical, thermal, pain, and itch information. These signals are transmitted via different types of peripheral afferent to the spinal cord, where they are extensively processed and integrated. $^{1,2}$ The resultant somatosensory signals are then sent to the brain by spinal projection neurons (SPNs), which represent key nodes in the somatosensory system. $^{1,3-5}$ Spinal projection neurons $(n = 785)$ S4: first order S10: higher order S10 VPL S17 S15 S19 SPNs are widely distributed in the spinal dorsal horn, with some also located in the lateral white matter (LWM), which includes the lateral cervical nucleus (LCN), the lateral spinal nucleus (LSN), and the lateral reticulated part of laminae 5/6 (L5/6).<sup>6</sup> Early studies using anterograde and retrograde tracing approaches have suggested the complexity of SPN projection patterns.<sup>7-10</sup> The majority of SPNs send axons that cross the midline and terminate in various brain regions, including the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM), nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS), parabrachial nucleus (PB), ventrolateral parts of the periaqueductal gray (PAG), ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus (VPL), ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM), and posterior complex of the thalamus (PO).

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Classification of spinal projection neurons To classify the SPNs, we first divided them into two categories: diencephalon-projecting neurons, which projected to thalamus and hypothalamus, and non-diencephalon-projecting neurons, which did not project to these areas. For diencephalon-projecting neurons, we performed hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and Ward's linkage based on their innervation strengths $(\ln(\text{number of terminals} + 1))$ in target thalamic and hypothalamic brain areas. For non-diencephalon-projecting neurons, we also performed hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and Ward's linkage based on their innervation strengths $(\ln(\text{number of terminals} + 1))$ in all target brain areas.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Limitations There are several limitations of this study. First, our projectome mapping was focused on neurons in C1-C4 spinal segments due to imaging constraints. Whether the knowledge obtained in this study applies to all spinal segments remains to be investigated. Second, some subtypes could be over- or underrepresented due to the limited sampling of neurons or the retrograde labeling approach. For example, the proportion of L1 SPNs observed in our dataset is less than that expected from some studies, $^{1,7,15,66}$ although another study suggests that L1 primarily consists of interneurons. $^{67}$ Third, although previous studies have shown a high reliability of the anterograde AAV2/1-CMV-Cre viral, $^{42}$ some non-specific labeling of spinally projecting neurons in the brain could occur via retrograde transport of this virus. As we only chose brain areas showing limited or no projection to the spinal cord, our overall conclusion would not be affected by the non-specific labeling. Fourth, since our projectome classification was based only on the patterns of targeted areas of each neuron, leaving variations in axon branching patterns within subtypes to be further explored. Finally, the transcriptomic identity of projectome-defined subtypes was not determined. In summary, we have characterized the diversity in the projection patterns of SPNs and central relay neurons, showing diverse hemispheric targeting preferences as well as extensive converging and divergent connectivity of individual neurons.

A recent study examined the projection patterns of PB relay neurons by bulk labeling and identified axons that arborized in many brain areas, including intralaminar thalamic nuclei (ILN), PAG, intermediate gray layer of the superior colliculus (InG), central amygdalar nucleus (CEA), and bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (BNST).[13] However, the projection patterns of central relay neurons are complex and likely to vary among neurons, and how a single PB relay neuron innervates its downstream brain areas remains unknown. Thus, whole-brain reconstruction of axon arbors with single-cell resolution is required to obtain a comprehensive understanding of how sensory information is conveyed to various brain areas by central relay neurons. Here, we sparsely labeled and reconstructed the morphology of 785 spinal cervical projection neurons and 1,464 central relay neurons that receive direct spinal inputs. Given the differential affinity of the virus to subtypes of neurons, some subtypes could be underrepresented. Nevertheless, our results have revealed new projection rules for these two types of neurons that form the core circuit of the somatosensory system based on the dataset with single-neuron resolution. [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] We first reconstructed the morphology of SPNs at the single-neuron level. Using a retrograde method, we sparsely labeled SPNs with EYFP (Figure 1A). Specifically, scRetro-AAV-Cre virus was injected into major targeted brain areas in the thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla (Figure 1A; Table S2), mainly including the external cuneate nucleus (ECU), CVLM, PB, pontine reticular nucleus, caudal part (PRNc), PAG, motor-related part of the superior colliculus (SCm), VPL, PO, mediodorsal nucleus of thalamus (MD), and lateral hypothalamic area (LHA). These targeted brain areas were selected according to previous findings[7,8,10,12,15] and were further validated through anterograde and retrograde tracing experiments (Figure S1). Subsequently, AAV-DIO-EYFP virus was injected into the dorsal horn of the cervical spinal cord (C1-C4 segments, Figure 1A), which was chosen for its proximity to the brain and to obtain sufficient coverage of neurons in a defined spinal area.

retrieved_docs: [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] SPN subtype coverage (Figures S3C-S3E). SPNs project widely in the hypothalamus, thalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla. We examined how these brain areas were co-innervated by individual SPNs and found that most SPNs co-innervated 2 or more brain regions, with $32\%$ innervating 5 regions (Figure 1E). On average, individual SPNs were arborized in 15 brain areas, ranging from 1 to 46 (Figure 1F; see STAR Methods). Notably, the midbrain reticular nucleus (MRN), SCm, and PAG received the most innervation (Figure S3F), with high co-innervation ratios (Figure S3G). These results demonstrate the prevalence of multiple target areas receiving innervation from individual SPNs, supporting the notion that individual SPNs can coordinate the activity of multiple downstream areas. Surprisingly, a few SPNs projected directly to the cortex (Figure S4A), a previously unreported finding further confirmed by observing the absence of EYFP-labeled cell bodies in brain samples (Figure S4B). This direct spino-cortical projection was also detected in samples with SPN bulk labeling (Figure S4C). Previous studies have identified multiple ascending spinal pathways. $^{5}$ One distinct aspect is whether they project to diencephalon. To analyze projection patterns of the SPNs at the single-neuron level, we first categorized SPNs into diencephalon-projecting and non-diencephalon-projecting groups.

Functional roles of these projections in sensory, affective, and motivational processing have been elucidated in rodents by optogenetic or pharmacogenetic methods.<sup>3,11-14</sup> Quantitative tracing using retrograde dyes (e.g., cholera toxin subunit B or Fluoro-Gold) and more recently using virally expressed fluorescent markers suggests that SPNs innervate multiple brain areas with diverse projection patterns.<sup>5,15,16</sup> Most SPNs project to contralateral brain regions, with some exhibiting bilateral or ipsilateral projections.<sup>3,7,10</sup> However, previous investigations into SPNs were limited either by a lack of single-cell resolution or by their coverage of only a few targeted brain areas. [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] Limitations of the study There are several limitations in our study. First, our dataset is still limited in the number of reconstructed neurons, as it covers a small fraction of actual cortical projection neurons in the mouse brain. The current strategy of sparse sampling may obscure the rare subtypes. More sophisticated intersectional strategies could improve the coverage of projection neurons. Second, the reproducibility of these projectome subtypes of cortical neurons is an important issue. Our definition of neuron subtypes still needs to be cross-validated with other methods.46 Third, for cortico-subcortical projections, although we mapped the finegrained projections from the cortex, these subcortical targets also receive inputs from the brain regions other than cortex. For example, striatum also receives inputs from thalamus. Therefore, a complete description of neural network is still lacking. Fourth, our definition of neuron subtypes was based mostly on the neuron morphologies. However, diverse neuronal subtypes have also been identified using the single-cell RNAseq method.6 Thus, further investigation of single-neuron morphology and gene expression of the same single neurons could characterize the neuronal diversity more comprehensively. Finally, the functional relevance of the projectome subtypes revealed in this study is still unclear.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Relationship between soma location, dendritic, and axon morphology The somatic and dendritic location of SPNs is important for determining sensory signal inputs, $^{1,5}$ and the central targets of their axonal projections likely depend on the sensory information they receive. However, the relationship between the soma location and the pattern of central axon targets of SPNs remains largely unclear. We found that soma and dendritic location of some projectome-defined SPNs subtypes exhibited strong preferences in specific areas or laminae of the dorsal spinal cord, although not for all subtypes. These data support that distinct projectome-defined SPNs subtypes could be differentially involved in transmitting various modalities of somatosensory formation. This is consistent with the fact that periphery sensory fibers processing different submodalities of somatosensory information terminate in different laninae. $^{1}$ We have also observed a correlation between axonal projection patterns and soma location for some thalamic relay neurons. An interesting question is whether a neuron achieve appropriate matching between dendritic inputs and axonal outputs, or vice versa. Our single-cell morphology reconstruction achieved a 3D view of the full morphology of SPNs. For the relationship between the total length of axon arbors and that of dendritic arbors, we revealed high correlation for 11 out of 19 projectome-defined SPN subtypes. Additionally, some projectome-defined subtypes exhibited obvious preference for specific dendritic patterns.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Limitations There are several limitations of this study. First, our projectome mapping was focused on neurons in C1-C4 spinal segments due to imaging constraints. Whether the knowledge obtained in this study applies to all spinal segments remains to be investigated. Second, some subtypes could be over- or underrepresented due to the limited sampling of neurons or the retrograde labeling approach. For example, the proportion of L1 SPNs observed in our dataset is less than that expected from some studies, $^{1,7,15,66}$ although another study suggests that L1 primarily consists of interneurons. $^{67}$ Third, although previous studies have shown a high reliability of the anterograde AAV2/1-CMV-Cre viral, $^{42}$ some non-specific labeling of spinally projecting neurons in the brain could occur via retrograde transport of this virus. As we only chose brain areas showing limited or no projection to the spinal cord, our overall conclusion would not be affected by the non-specific labeling. [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Relationship between soma location, dendritic, and axon morphology The somatic and dendritic location of SPNs is important for determining sensory signal inputs, $^{1,5}$ and the central targets of their axonal projections likely depend on the sensory information they receive. However, the relationship between the soma location and the pattern of central axon targets of SPNs remains largely unclear. We found that soma and dendritic location of some projectome-defined SPNs subtypes exhibited strong preferences in specific areas or laminae of the dorsal spinal cord, although not for all subtypes. These data support that distinct projectome-defined SPNs subtypes could be differentially involved in transmitting various modalities of somatosensory formation. This is consistent with the fact that periphery sensory fibers processing different submodalities of somatosensory information terminate in different laninae. $^{1}$ We have also observed a correlation between axonal projection patterns and soma location for some thalamic relay neurons. An interesting question is whether a neuron achieve appropriate matching between dendritic inputs and axonal outputs, or vice versa. Our single-cell morphology reconstruction achieved a 3D view of the full morphology of SPNs. For the relationship between the total length of axon arbors and that of dendritic arbors, we revealed high correlation for 11 out of 19 projectome-defined SPN subtypes. Additionally, some projectome-defined subtypes exhibited obvious preference for specific dendritic patterns.

Although previous studies have described the two-dimensional (2D) dendritic morphology of SPNs, $^{7,35,36}$ the whole dendritic morphology and the relationship between dendrites and axons of individual SPNs remain elusive. Using fMOST, we reconstructed the full three-dimensional (3D) dendritic morphology of 753 SPNs (Figures 2A and 2B) and observed significant regional variations in dendritic length, with the longest $(3.5 \pm 1.2 \mathrm{~mm})$ for SPNs in L5/6 and the shortest $(2.4 \pm 1.6 \mathrm{~mm})$ for SPNs in L1/2 (Figure 2C). Importantly, dendritic and axonal arbor length showed correlations in 11 out of 19 subtypes $(p < 0.05$ , Pearson correlation) (Figures S7B and S7C), indicating a coordinated development of dendritic and axonal arbors. To explore dendritic morphology more comprehensively, we categorized SPNs based on their soma location into four groups: superficial, deep, LWM, and MWM. These groups were further divided into 15 clusters using NBLAST $^{37}$ (Figures 2D, 2E, and S7D; Video S2). Dendritic differences between clusters were further examined by 3D polarity averages (Figure 2F).

retrieved_docs: [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Parallel versus convergent/divergent processing of somatosensory information While different modalities of somatosensory information are likely to be processed by distinct neurons at the level of peripheral nerves and spinal cord, there are interactions among different sensory modalities during central processing, particularly at the level of sensory perception.[65] The single-cell projection analysis allows us to determine whether there is structural basis, including parallel and convergent/divergent projection patterns, to explain the separate and interacting somatosensory information processing along ascending pathways. For parallel projection patterns, we found that the contralateral-only and ipsilateral-only projectome subtypes of SPNs could send somatosensory information to the brain in parallel for independent processing. Moreover, we identified parallel spinal-lateral SCm-contralateral brainstem, and spinal-medial SCm-ipsilateral brainstem pathways. We speculate that these two parallel pathways may be involved in processing information associated with orienting and defensive behaviors.[31,49,50] Additionally, thalamic relay neurons also parallelly relay signals to the sensory, motor, and higher-order cortical areas through distinct channels. However, most if not all subtypes, including the ones mentioned above, projected to multiple cortical and subcortical brain areas, suggesting a prevalent divergent projections. These divergent collateral projections consequently led to a convergence of projections in various brain areas.

Whether the knowledge obtained in this study applies to all spinal segments remains to be investigated. Second, some subtypes could be over- or underrepresented due to the limited sampling of neurons or the retrograde labeling approach. For example, the proportion of L1 SPNs observed in our dataset is less than that expected from some studies, $^{1,7,15,66}$ although another study suggests that L1 primarily consists of interneurons. $^{67}$ Third, although previous studies have shown a high reliability of the anterograde AAV2/1-CMV-Cre viral, $^{42}$ some non-specific labeling of spinally projecting neurons in the brain could occur via retrograde transport of this virus. Fourth, since our projectome classification was based only on the patterns of targeted areas of each neuron, leaving variations in axon branching patterns within subtypes to be further explored. [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] INTRODUCTION The somatosensory system plays critical roles in processing diverse sensory signals that encode mechanical, thermal, pain, and itch information. These signals are transmitted via different types of peripheral afferent to the spinal cord, where they are extensively processed and integrated. $^{1,2}$ The resultant somatosensory signals are then sent to the brain by spinal projection neurons (SPNs), which represent key nodes in the somatosensory system. $^{1,3-5}$ Spinal projection neurons $(n = 785)$ S4: first order S10: higher order S10 VPL S17 S15 S19 SPNs are widely distributed in the spinal dorsal horn, with some also located in the lateral white matter (LWM), which includes the lateral cervical nucleus (LCN), the lateral spinal nucleus (LSN), and the lateral reticulated part of laminae 5/6 (L5/6).<sup>6</sup> Early studies using anterograde and retrograde tracing approaches have suggested the complexity of SPN projection patterns.<sup>7-10</sup> The majority of SPNs send axons that cross the midline and terminate in various brain regions, including the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM), nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS), parabrachial nucleus (PB), ventrolateral parts of the periaqueductal gray (PAG), ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus (VPL), ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM), and posterior complex of the thalamus (PO).

These labeled images were then interpolated along the axial direction to construct the 3D spinal cord template. The manually labeled annotations and the interpolated annotations were stacked together to reconstruct the spinal atlas template in a three-dimensional space. After that, we manually marked a set of points representing the locations of 14 dorsal root of the cervical segment. The grey values from the image and the coordinate information from the points were used together as the similarity measurement. We have reconstructed mouse cervical spinal projection neurons at single-cell resolution and identified 19 projectome-defined subtypes exhibiting diverse projection patterns. We also reconstructed the brain-wide axonal projections of central relay neurons that receive direct spinal inputs at the single-cell resolution. We discovered parallel, divergent, and convergent projection patterns for spinal projection neurons and central relay neurons. Our results revealed the diverse pathways channeling spinal information to the cortex. Furthermore, we identified parallel lateral and medial spinal-superior colliculus-brainstem pathways, which could be involved in orienting and defensive behaviors, respectively. These data allowed us to construct a wiring diagram for ascending somatosensory pathways with projectome-defined subtype resolution. Our single-cell projectome analysis provided a new framework for understanding the complex neural circuitry underlying coordinated processing of diverse somatosensory modalities.

[source: Jiao et al - 2025 - Projectome-based characterization of hypothalamic peptidergic neurons in male mice.md] Statistics and reproducibility No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size, and the experiments were not randomized. For single-neuron projectome data, Supplementary Fig. 1a shows the procedure for sample exclusion. In brief, investigators were blinded to the identity of the brain samples being processed. Brain samples with excessively dense labeling, which precludes single-axon tracing, were excluded from subsequent neuronal tracing procedures. All traced neurons underwent multiple rounds of manual verification to ensure accuracy. Neurons with erroneous tracing data were excluded from further analysis. Additionally, neurons with soma locations outside the hypothalamus were excluded unless otherwise stated. All other neurons included for analysis in the present study had explicitly stated identifiers (for example, soma location, neuropeptide population or target regions). For EASI-FISH experiments, brain slices from two independently injected male mice (biological replicates) were processed for imaging and grouped for analysis, following the standard protocol for single-neuron analysis. For all other histological studies, at least three biological replicates were obtained for each experiment. For a detailed summary of the statistical analysis, see Supplementary Table 6.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] The surgery was performed following the protocols published previously.13 Briefly, mice were anesthetized with the mixture of Zoletil (Tiletamine hydrochloride: 15 mg/kg; Zalazepam hydrochloride: 15 mg/kg; purchased from Virbac S.A) and Xylazine hydrochloride (80 mg/kg, purchased from Huamu Veterinary Medicine Co., Ltd.). For intra-brain virus injection, the skull was exposed by midline scalp incision, and craniotomy ( $\sim 1.5$ mm diameter) was made using a hand-held drill for the introduction of microinjection glass pipette according to the coordinates of target brain regions. Viruses were injected into target brain areas at the rate of $\sim 20\mathrm{nL / min}$ using an air-pressure system (Picospritzer III, Parker) or oil-pressure system (Narishige Scientific Instrument Lab). After the completion of virus injection, the glass pipette was left in place for $\sim 5$ min and then withdrew slowly to avoid back-flow of virus. After that, we sutured the skin and put animals on a heating blanket before returning them back to their home cages. For intra-spinal cord virus injection, vertebrae of mice were exposed at C1-C4 and fixed on the stereotaxic frame. For exposure of the spinal cord, the dura was incised using the anatomy needle. A microinjection glass pipette was induced to the spinal dorsal horn with the degree of 30. Virus was delivered into the dorsal spinal cord at the rate of $\sim 10\mathrm{~nL/min}$.

Mice were raised under standard conditions (12-hour light/dark cycle, $22 - 25^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $30 - 70\%$ humidity) with access to food and water ad libitum. Virus injection. To achieve sparse labeling, a mixture of a diluted virus expressing Cre-recombinase (AAV2/8-hSyn-Cre-WPRE-pA, original titer: $1.41 \times 10^{13}$ viral genomes per milliliter) and a Cre-recombinase dependent reporter virus (AAV2/8-CAG-Flex-EGFP-WPRE-pA, original titer: $1.25 \times 10^{13}$ viral genomes per milliliter) were injected into the different PFC regions of adult C57BL/6 male mice. For each injection site, $20 - 50\mathrm{nl}$ of virus mixture was injected. The coordinates of stereotaxic injection were chosen according to The Mouse Brain in Stereotaxic Coordinates (2nd edition), measured in anterior-posterior (AP), medial-lateral (ML) and dorsal-ventral (DV) directions. The angle of micro-injection is relative to the vertical plane of the DV axis. The bregma point is defined as $0^{\circ}$ $(0,0,0)$ in the coordinate system of vertical injection. For in vivo stereotaxic injections, mice were deeply anaesthetized with $0.14\mathrm{g / kg}$ pentobarbital sodium. Viruses were injected unilaterally into the PVH (bregma: $-0.8\mathrm{mm}$ ; lateral: $-0.65\mathrm{mm}$ ; ventral: $4.3\mathrm{mm}$ ) of Oxt-ires-Cre mice using a digital stereotaxic instrument (RWD Instruments, China). For bulk labeling of neurons, 300 nl of rAAV (2/9)-EF1 $\alpha$ -DIO-YPet-p2A-mGFP was injected into the PVH of virgin female, lactating female and male Oxt-ires-Cre mice at 70 nl/min, using a syringe pump (Harvard Apparatus). This dose labels nearly all PVH OXT neurons on the injection side, without labeling SO neurons. To label NTS projecting C2 neurons, 200 nI CTB (1.0 mg/ml, Alexa Fluor 555 conjugate, Invitrogen, Cat# C34776) was injected bilaterally into NTS (bregma: $-7.80\mathrm{mm}$ ; lateral: $-0.33\mathrm{mm}$ ; ventral: $3.5\mathrm{mm}$ ) at 20 nI/min using a syringe pump (Harvard Apparatus).

Categorical data, such as brain annotation from the ABA, can also be incorporated. After loading the brain annotation file, the brain area annotation at any chosen position in the brain can be indicated. FNT tracing process consists of three steps: finding a putative path, examining the putative path and extending the current neurite tree, as summarized in Extended Data Fig. 1b. In FNT, we included a new operation: finding a putative path only with a starting position. In FNT, users' confirmation at each step ensures the correctness of tracing. After users confirm that a branch is traced to the end, the branch is marked as finished. FNT keeps the records of all unfinished branches and will automatically jump to the nearest unfinished branch when the current branch is finished. A neuron tree can be traversed in this way until it is completed. Users can easily edit existing branches or un-do previous unwanted operations. A demonstration of FNT tracing process is shown in Supplementary Video 1. Quality control and evaluation. To ensure the validity of tracing result, every neuron was traced by two independent human tracers. Then, the results were merged by a third human tracer. We designed a scoring scheme combining different types of errors to evaluate the quality of tracing result.

[source: Jiao et al - 2025 - Projectome-based characterization of hypothalamic peptidergic neurons in male mice.md] Data analysis Neuron exclusion. All neurons were manually checked to ensure that they were correctly traced. Neurons found to have erroneous tracing data were excluded from further analysis. Additionally, neurons whose soma location was outside the hypothalamus were also excluded for clustering analysis. In total, we included 7,180 neurons in our analysis with neuronal cell body located in the Allen CCFv3-defined hypothalamus. We mirrored all neurons to the same hemisphere before the analysis procedures. Parameter calculation. Based on the standard Allen CCFv3 annotation file ( we calculated the soma location, axon length and terminal number for each neuron in each brain region using a self-developed Python library ( To analyze and show the data in a more reader-friendly way, we manually combined some brain areas into larger ones. Calculating the total brain volume occupation. We divided the standard mouse brain (CCFv3) into small cubes of $25\mu \mathrm{m} \times 25\mu \mathrm{m} \times 25\mu \mathrm{m}$. Subsequently, we determined whether each cube has an axon projection signal from the 7,180 reconstructed neurons. We found that the total axon arbors of these peptidergic neurons extended to occupy approximately $21.8\%$ and $10.2\%$ of the voxels on the ipsilateral and contralateral sides of the brain, respectively. Neuron visualization. All 3D neuron showcases were plotted using a self-developed Python package, 'neuron-vis' ( Colors were randomly assigned to individual neurons plotted at a population level.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Signal to noise ratio (SNR) analysis We analyzed the SNR according to the protocol published previously.24 Briefly, the straight-line distance from each node in the SWC file to the soma point (root node) was calculated and the nodes with an integer multiple of the sampling distance $(40\mu m)$ were selected as sampling points. Each sampling point was defined as the center, and six neighboring pixels for the axonal end or eight neighboring pixels for the axon were obtained as the range. The mean pixel grayscale value of the range was calculated as average signal intensity. Then, SNR is calculated using difference in intensity between the axons/axonal-ends with their surrounding background, divided by the standard deviation of background. The median SNRs for every $0.5\mathrm{mm}$ neuronal segment were calculated.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] TB-sized CH1 images were processed into one million data cubes with $256 \times 256 \times 90$ voxels using the FNT-slice2cube program of the Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT) software.[26] Cubes used for projectome reconstruction were then compressed with the high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) method. The raw data was down-sampled to the resolution of $20 \times 20 \times 20\mu \mathrm{m}^3$ for the overview of the whole-brain data. FNT was used for reconstruction of the full morphology of neurons as described previously.[26,71] During tracing, the cube that users selected was loaded into the computer memory automatically and visualized in 3D by maximal intensity projection algorithm. FNT tracing process is semi-automatic: 1) a putative path can be found by A-star algorithm only with a starting position; 2) the human tracers will confirm and make revision manually. All neurons were reconstructed by two independent experienced tracers; then these two reconstructed results were merged and examined by another experienced person to obtain the final results. In our tracing process, only neurons with tracing score higher than 90 were included for further analysis. The neuron tracing score was calculated based on the protocols published previously.[26]

question: Which algorithm was used to compute the similarity matrix for dendritic morphology clustering of spinal projection neurons?
retrieved_docs: [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Classification of dendrites based on their morphology Dendrites of SPNs (except for neurons in L1/2) were hierarchically clustered using Euclidean distance and Ward's linkage based on similarity matrix obtained from NBLAST algorithm.37 Briefly, somata of all neurons were moved to the same starting point before using the NBLAST algorithm to calculate the similarity matrix to avoid the effect of soma location on the dendritic clustering.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Columns clustering analysis of the SCm projections from SPNs First, we utilized annotation information provided by Allen CCFv3 to directly project the left hemisphere SCm onto a horizontal plane, obtaining the coordinates of the projected voxels. Then, employing the k-means method for clustering, we set $K = 50$ and partitioned the left SCm into 50 units of equal area. Subsequently, we propagated the labels of these voxel units along the direction perpendicular to the horizontal plane throughout the entire three-dimensional SCm, resulting in 50 columnar units in SCm. Next, we computed the axonal length from all spinal cord projecting single cells to each columnar unit, based on a standardized connection matrix $(ln(axon\ length + 1))$. Then we utilized hierarchical clustering to classify neurons using Euclidean distance and Ward's linkage.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Columns clustering analysis of cortical projection of thalamic relay neurons To divide cortex into a series of similar columns, we first partitioned the cortex surface into patches $(n = 200)$ using k-means method. Then, these labels of patches were propagated to the whole cortex volume along the laminae direction based on the 'streamline' method.[26] The projection strengths in each cortical columns of all thalamic relay neurons were calculated instead of the analyses of the projection strengths in each brain region. Projection strengths in all columns constituted the projectome of each neuron. We applied hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and Ward's linkage, based on this connection matrix to identify neuron subtypes.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Relationship between dendritic and axonal morphology of SPNs Dendrites of SPNs are critical for integrating somatosensory inputs. Although previous studies have described the two-dimensional (2D) dendritic morphology of SPNs, $^{7,35,36}$ the whole dendritic morphology and the relationship between dendrites and axons of individual SPNs remain elusive. Using fMOST, we reconstructed the full three-dimensional (3D) dendritic morphology of 753 SPNs (Figures 2A and 2B) and observed significant regional variations in dendritic length, with the longest $(3.5 \pm 1.2 \mathrm{~mm})$ for SPNs in L5/6 and the shortest $(2.4 \pm 1.6 \mathrm{~mm})$ for SPNs in L1/2 (Figure 2C). Dendritic distribution patterns also varied across laminae: dendrites of SPNs in L1/2 extended to L3, SPNs in L3 reached superficial laminae, while SPNs in L4–L6 were restricted to deep laminae (Figure S7A). Importantly, dendritic and axonal arbor length showed correlations in 11 out of 19 subtypes $(p < 0.05$ , Pearson correlation) (Figures S7B and S7C), indicating a coordinated development of dendritic and axonal arbors. To explore dendritic morphology more comprehensively, we categorized SPNs based on their soma location into four groups: superficial, deep, LWM, and MWM. These groups were further divided into 15 clusters using NBLAST $^{37}$ (Figures 2D, 2E, and S7D; Video S2). Dendritic differences between clusters were further examined by 3D polarity averages (Figure 2F).

A new software tool, Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT), was developed in-house to trace long-range axon projection in terabyte datasets generated by light microscopy[26]. In brief, the original image data are split into smaller three-dimensional (3D) data cubes by a program called 'slice2cube' in FNT. At any time, approximately eight neighboring cubes around a position are loaded into computer memory automatically and visualized in 3D for tracing. [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Limitations There are several limitations of this study. First, our projectome mapping was focused on neurons in C1-C4 spinal segments due to imaging constraints. Whether the knowledge obtained in this study applies to all spinal segments remains to be investigated. Second, some subtypes could be over- or underrepresented due to the limited sampling of neurons or the retrograde labeling approach. For example, the proportion of L1 SPNs observed in our dataset is less than that expected from some studies, $^{1,7,15,66}$ although another study suggests that L1 primarily consists of interneurons. $^{67}$ Third, although previous studies have shown a high reliability of the anterograde AAV2/1-CMV-Cre viral, $^{42}$ some non-specific labeling of spinally projecting neurons in the brain could occur via retrograde transport of this virus. As we only chose brain areas showing limited or no projection to the spinal cord, our overall conclusion would not be affected by the non-specific labeling. Fourth, since our projectome classification was based only on the patterns of targeted areas of each neuron, leaving variations in axon branching patterns within subtypes to be further explored. Finally, the transcriptomic identity of projectome-defined subtypes was not determined. In summary, we have characterized the diversity in the projection patterns of SPNs and central relay neurons, showing diverse hemispheric targeting preferences as well as extensive converging and divergent connectivity of individual neurons.

question: How is the maximum depth of an axonal edge assigned, and what defines the axonal trunk based on this depth?
retrieved_docs: [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Definition of axonal trunk and terminal branches We defined a neuron tree hierarchy by assigning an order and depth for each axonal edge. The first axon edge from the soma is labeled as order 0, the following children edges with axon length longer than one-tenth of the maximum children edge and the bifurcation angle smaller than 45 degrees were labeled as parent's order, otherwise labeled as parent's order plus one. We repeated this process until all edges were labeled with an order. To determine the maximum depth of each edge, we set the terminal edge as depth 0 and the depth of its parent edge was defined according to its relationship with the children edges with maximum depth. If the order of parents edges was higher, then the depth of the parent edge plus one, otherwise similar with that of the children edges with maximum depth. We iterated this process for all edges. The axonal trunk was defined as the edges with the maximum depth greater than half of maximum depth of the entire neuron, or that with the maximum path from the branch point to all downstream terminal points is longer than one-tenth of the maximum path from root to all the terminals. Additionally, axon arbors were defined as the portion of edges that exclude the axonal trunk.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Signal to noise ratio (SNR) analysis We analyzed the SNR according to the protocol published previously.24 Briefly, the straight-line distance from each node in the SWC file to the soma point (root node) was calculated and the nodes with an integer multiple of the sampling distance $(40\mu m)$ were selected as sampling points. Each sampling point was defined as the center, and six neighboring pixels for the axonal end or eight neighboring pixels for the axon were obtained as the range. The mean pixel grayscale value of the range was calculated as average signal intensity. Then, SNR is calculated using difference in intensity between the axons/axonal-ends with their surrounding background, divided by the standard deviation of background. The median SNRs for every $0.5\mathrm{mm}$ neuronal segment were calculated.

For PT neurons, in early development, their primary axons extended ventrally to spinal cord, whereas, in later development, primary axons of partial neurons were retracted and ended in hindbrain $^{52}$. [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] INTRODUCTION The somatosensory system plays critical roles in processing diverse sensory signals that encode mechanical, thermal, pain, and itch information. These signals are transmitted via different types of peripheral afferent to the spinal cord, where they are extensively processed and integrated. $^{1,2}$ The resultant somatosensory signals are then sent to the brain by spinal projection neurons (SPNs), which represent key nodes in the somatosensory system. $^{1,3-5}$ Spinal projection neurons $(n = 785)$ S4: first order S10: higher order S10 VPL S17 S15 S19 SPNs are widely distributed in the spinal dorsal horn, with some also located in the lateral white matter (LWM), which includes the lateral cervical nucleus (LCN), the lateral spinal nucleus (LSN), and the lateral reticulated part of laminae 5/6 (L5/6).<sup>6</sup> Early studies using anterograde and retrograde tracing approaches have suggested the complexity of SPN projection patterns.<sup>7-10</sup> The majority of SPNs send axons that cross the midline and terminate in various brain regions, including the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM), nucleus of the solitary tract (NTS), parabrachial nucleus (PB), ventrolateral parts of the periaqueductal gray (PAG), ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus (VPL), ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus (VPM), and posterior complex of the thalamus (PO).

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Spinal projection neurons (legend on next page) To further examine the heterogeneity in the projection patterns of PB relay neurons, we pooled contralateral and ipsilateral PB relay neurons together by flipping PB neurons in the right side to the left hemisphere and classified these neurons into 7 subtypes based on their projection targets and axon arbor length in each target area (Figure 4D; Video S7). Among these subtypes, PB_1 and PB_2 had major projections in the MD via contralateral and ipsilateral routes, respectively (Figures 4D-4F and S11B). These MD-projecting subtypes likely could be involved in cognitive aspects of somatosensation. Subtypes PB_5 and PB_6 mainly projected to the medulla. Differing from the simple projection patterns of subtype PB_6, subtype PB_5 sent collaterals to forebrain areas, the hypothalamus, and midbrain areas SCm and MRN (Figures 4D-4F and S11B). We found that brain regions MRN, PAG, and pedunculopontine nucleus (PPN) were common downstream targets for neurons in most subtypes (Figure S11C). The soma location of PB subtypes also exhibited different distribution patterns. We found that MD-projecting subtypes were located mainly in the dorsal lateral PB, while brainstem-projecting subtypes were located mainly in the ventral PB (Figure S11D). For the lateralization of projections, we found that most subtypes—except for subtype PB_6, which had an ipsilateral-dominant projection—had bilateral projections (Figures 4D and 4G).

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Classification of spinal projection neurons To classify the SPNs, we first divided them into two categories: diencephalon-projecting neurons, which projected to thalamus and hypothalamus, and non-diencephalon-projecting neurons, which did not project to these areas. For diencephalon-projecting neurons, we performed hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and Ward's linkage based on their innervation strengths $(\ln(\text{number of terminals} + 1))$ in target thalamic and hypothalamic brain areas. For non-diencephalon-projecting neurons, we also performed hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and Ward's linkage based on their innervation strengths $(\ln(\text{number of terminals} + 1))$ in all target brain areas.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] SUMMARY Relay of multimodal somatosensory information from the spinal cord to the brain is critical for sensory perception, but the underlying circuit organization remains unclear. We have reconstructed mouse cervical spinal projection neurons at single-cell resolution and identified 19 projectome-defined subtypes exhibiting diverse projection patterns. We also reconstructed the brain-wide axonal projections of central relay neurons that receive direct spinal inputs at the single-cell resolution. We discovered parallel, divergent, and convergent projection patterns for spinal projection neurons and central relay neurons. Our results revealed the diverse pathways channeling spinal information to the cortex. Furthermore, we identified parallel lateral and medial spinal-superior colliculus-brainstem pathways, which could be involved in orienting and defensive behaviors, respectively. These data allowed us to construct a wiring diagram for ascending somatosensory pathways with projectome-defined subtype resolution. Our single-cell projectome analysis provided a new framework for understanding the complex neural circuitry underlying coordinated processing of diverse somatosensory modalities.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] nd several single-neuron projectome analyses,[22,23] these studies did not focus on thalamic relay neurons specifically. A recent study examined the projection patterns of PB relay neurons by bulk labeling and identified axons that arborized in many brain areas, including intralaminar thalamic nuclei (ILN), PAG, intermediate gray layer of the superior colliculus (InG), central amygdalar nucleus (CEA), and bed nuclei of the stria terminalis (BNST).[13] However, the projection patterns of central relay neurons are complex and likely to vary among neurons, and how a single PB relay neuron innervates its downstream brain areas remains unknown. Thus, whole-brain reconstruction of axon arbors with single-cell resolution is required to obtain a comprehensive understanding of how sensory information is conveyed to various brain areas by central relay neurons. Here, we sparsely labeled and reconstructed the morphology of 785 spinal cervical projection neurons and 1,464 central relay neurons that receive direct spinal inputs. Given the differential affinity of the virus to subtypes of neurons, some subtypes could be underrepresented. Nevertheless, our results have revealed new projection rules for these two types of neurons that form the core circuit of the somatosensory system based on the dataset with single-neuron resolution. Our dataset (accessible at offers a structural framework for understanding diverse but coordinated functions of the somatosensory system. [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Limitations There are several limitations of this study. First, our projectome mapping was focused on neurons in C1-C4 spinal segments due to imaging constraints. Whether the knowledge obtained in this study applies to all spinal segments remains to be investigated. Second, some subtypes could be over- or underrepresented due to the limited sampling of neurons or the retrograde labeling approach. For example, the proportion of L1 SPNs observed in our dataset is less than that expected from some studies, $^{1,7,15,66}$ although another study suggests that L1 primarily consists of interneurons. $^{67}$ Third, although previous studies have shown a high reliability of the anterograde AAV2/1-CMV-Cre viral, $^{42}$ some non-specific labeling of spinally projecting neurons in the brain could occur via retrograde transport of this virus. As we only chose brain areas showing limited or no projection to the spinal cord, our overall conclusion would not be affected by the non-specific labeling. Fourth, since our projectome classification was based only on the patterns of targeted areas of each neuron, leaving variations in axon branching patterns within subtypes to be further explored. Finally, the transcriptomic identity of projectome-defined subtypes was not determined. In summary, we have characterized the diversity in the projection patterns of SPNs and central relay neurons, showing diverse hemispheric targeting preferences as well as extensive converging and divergent connectivity of individual neurons.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Relationship between soma location, dendritic, and axon morphology The somatic and dendritic location of SPNs is important for determining sensory signal inputs, $^{1,5}$ and the central targets of their axonal projections likely depend on the sensory information they receive. However, the relationship between the soma location and the pattern of central axon targets of SPNs remains largely unclear. We found that soma and dendritic location of some projectome-defined SPNs subtypes exhibited strong preferences in specific areas or laminae of the dorsal spinal cord, although not for all subtypes. These data support that distinct projectome-defined SPNs subtypes could be differentially involved in transmitting various modalities of somatosensory formation. This is consistent with the fact that periphery sensory fibers processing different submodalities of somatosensory information terminate in different laninae. $^{1}$ We have also observed a correlation between axonal projection patterns and soma location for some thalamic relay neurons. An interesting question is whether a neuron achieve appropriate matching between dendritic inputs and axonal outputs, or vice versa. Our single-cell morphology reconstruction achieved a 3D view of the full morphology of SPNs. For the relationship between the total length of axon arbors and that of dendritic arbors, we revealed high correlation for 11 out of 19 projectome-defined SPN subtypes. Additionally, some projectome-defined subtypes exhibited obvious preference for specific dendritic patterns.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] We first reconstructed the morphology of SPNs at the single-neuron level. Using a retrograde method, we sparsely labeled SPNs with EYFP (Figure 1A). Specifically, scRetro-AAV-Cre virus was injected into major targeted brain areas in the thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, pons, and medulla (Figure 1A; Table S2), mainly including the external cuneate nucleus (ECU), CVLM, PB, pontine reticular nucleus, caudal part (PRNc), PAG, motor-related part of the superior colliculus (SCm), VPL, PO, mediodorsal nucleus of thalamus (MD), and lateral hypothalamic area (LHA). These targeted brain areas were selected according to previous findings[7,8,10,12,15] and were further validated through anterograde and retrograde tracing experiments (Figure S1). Subsequently, AAV-DIO-EYFP virus was injected into the dorsal horn of the cervical spinal cord (C1-C4 segments, Figure 1A), which was chosen for its proximity to the brain and to obtain sufficient coverage of neurons in a defined spinal area.
answer: Spinal projection neurons (SPNs) were classified into diencephalon-projecting and non-diencephalon-projecting neurons, then further subdivided using hierarchical clustering based on innervation strengths. The transcriptomic identity of these subtypes was not determined.

question: What imaging technique was used to acquire the brain and spinal cord datasets, and what software was employed for full neuronal morphology reconstruction?
retrieved_docs: [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] TB-sized CH1 images were processed into one million data cubes with $256 \times 256 \times 90$ voxels using the FNT-slice2cube program of the Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT) software.[26] Cubes used for projectome reconstruction were then compressed with the high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) method. The raw data was down-sampled to the resolution of $20 \times 20 \times 20\mu \mathrm{m}^3$ for the overview of the whole-brain data. FNT was used for reconstruction of the full morphology of neurons as described previously.[26,71] During tracing, the cube that users selected was loaded into the computer memory automatically and visualized in 3D by maximal intensity projection algorithm. FNT tracing process is semi-automatic: 1) a putative path can be found by A-star algorithm only with a starting position; 2) the human tracers will confirm and make revision manually. All neurons were reconstructed by two independent experienced tracers; then these two reconstructed results were merged and examined by another experienced person to obtain the final results. In our tracing process, only neurons with tracing score higher than 90 were included for further analysis. The neuron tracing score was calculated based on the protocols published previously.[26]

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography (fMOST) imaging The EYFP-labeled tissue was first embedded with HM20 resin (Electron Microscopy Sciences, cat.no.14340) to preserve the structure and provide stability. To recover the resin-embedded EYFP fluorescence, $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ was added to the imaging water bath for chemical reactivation, propidium iodide (PI) was add for nuclei staining.70 Dual channel fMOST imaging systems were then applied to acquire the image datasets of the whole brain and spinal cord.24,25 The green channel of the system was used to obtain the EYFP signals of neural structures (CH1), and the red channel was used to obtain the propidium iodide (PI) labeled cytoarchitectural information (CH2). As the sample contained both the spinal cord and brain, making the image volume much larger than usual (15-20 TB size), consisting of approximately 14,000 coronal planes with lateral (XY) resolution of $0.32\mu m$ or $0.35\mu m$ , and axial (Z) resolution of $1\mu m$. The obtained image datasets were then resampled to isotropic $1\mu m$ resolution for further template construction and image registration.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Registration of datasets to the template We developed registration strategies of our acquired brain-spinal cord datasets for various downstream analyses. To quantitatively analyze data in the brain, we mapped our reconstructed neurons onto CCFv3. The recognizable anatomical regions of the brain were chosen from the acquired image datasets and segmented as registration landmarks based on the cytoarchitectonic information provided by PI staining. Using Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs), we acquired transformation parameters by applying affine transformation and symmetric image normalization to the segmented landmarks.[28] These parameters were used for both neuron registration and high-resolution image registration. To quantitatively analyze data in the spinal cord, we mapped the reconstructed SPNs in the 3D spinal cord template. We marked as many dorsal roots from the acquired datasets as possible, although not all dorsal roots could be recognized. The outline and dorsal roots' coordinates of the spinal cord were served as landmarks during the nonlinear registration process. Briefly, we adjusted the posture of the dataset using the dorsal roots' coordinates of the template and dataset, and then nonlinearly transformed the dataset to the template, like brain registration strategy previously mentioned. Also, the unified template constructed in the previous part could also be regarded as an extended brain atlas, consisting of a brain image from CCFv3, and a brain-spinal cord image from the spinal cord template.

[source: Li et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectomes of mouse paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus oxytocin neurons reveal mutually exclusive projection patterns.md] Whole-brain images of sparse labeling samples were acquired using fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography (fMOST) technology. The raw image dataset of each sample includes two channels: the GFP channel (channel 1, CH1) contains morphological information of labeled neurons, while the propidium iodide (PI) channel (channel 2, CH2) contains cytoarchitectonic information. Each dataset has approximately 10000 raw images of $30000 \times 20000$ pixels of both CH1 and CH2, with a voxel resolution of $0.35 \times 0.35 \times 1.0 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$. The coordinate system of raw images is kept consistent in all subsequent processing. The X, Y and Z values of coordinates increased in value along the right-left (X), dorsal-ventral (Y) and anterior-posterior (Z) directions. TB-sized CH1 raw images were divided into one million data cubes of $256 \times 256 \times 100$ voxels using the FNT-slice2cube command of the Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT) software,[25] compressed using the high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) method for reconstruction. CH1 images were downsampled to a resolution of $20 \times 20 \times 20 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$ in the whole-brain projection overview to facilitate identification of the reconstruction start point.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Spinal cord template construction and integration To build a 3D spinal cord template, we manually labeled the anatomical structures of the spinal cord first, including the gray and white matter, distinct laminae of the gray matter and the central canal, according to the 2D atlas from Allen Brain ( in every 100 coronal planes selected from the image sequence at $20~\mu \mathrm{m}$ resolution. retrieved_docs: [source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] INTRODUCTION Opioids have been used for pain relief for thousands of years and are the most powerful painkillers. Opioid receptors and their ligands are widely expressed in the pain pathway, indicating the potential role of endogenously produced opioid peptides in modulating pain processing [1,2]. The analgesic effect of endogenous opioids has been demonstrated in many pharmacological studies [3-5]. Recent studies have also shown that neurons involved in endogenous opioid analgesia in inflammatory pain are distinct from those involved in exogenous opioids [6]. Thus, in addition to the use of opioid-related analgesic drugs, enhancing endogenous opioid analgesia by targeting endogenous opioid release or the underlying circuits could be an alternative approach to pain management. In this study, we aimed to elu cidate the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception, a type of endogenous analgesia that contributes to the resolution of hyperalgesia and is mediated by the mu-opioid receptor (MOR), which is known to play a dominant role in exogenous and endogenous opioid analgesia [6-8].

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] ABSTRACT Endogenous opioid antinociception is a self-regulatory mechanism that reduces chronic pain, but its underlying circuit mechanism remains largely unknown. Here, we showed that endogenous opioid antinociception required the activation of mu-opioid receptors (MORs) in GABAergic neurons of the central amygdala nucleus (CEA) in a persistent-hyperalgesia mouse model. Pharmacogenetic suppression of these $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which mimics the effect of MOR activation, alleviated the persistent hyperalgesia. Furthermore, single-neuron projection analysis revealed multiple projectome-based subtypes of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, each innervating distinct target brain regions. We found that the suppression of axon branches projecting to the parabrachial nucleus (PB) of one subtype of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons alleviated persistent hyperalgesia, indicating a subtype- and axonal-branch-specific mechanism of action. Further electrophysiological analysis revealed that suppression of a distinct CEA-PB disinhibitory circuit controlled endogenous opioid antinociception. Thus, this study identified the central neural circuit that underlies endogenous opioid antinociception, providing new insight into the endogenous pain modulatory mechanisms. This mechanism might not be involved in CEA, as we found that endogenous opioid antinociception was blocked by neutral MOR antagonists CTAP and $6\beta$ -naltrexol, which are known to be ineffective in blocking constitutively active MORs. [source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] DISCUSSION In this study, we identified a neural circuit that was essential for mediating endogenous opioid antinociception during CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. We found that endogenous opioid antinociception was mediated by MORs expressed in CEA inhibitory projection neurons. Using single-neuron projectome analysis, we defined the projection subtypes of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, each of which could project to multiple brain regions. Based on the projectome patterns of single $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, we showed that PB-projecting axon branches of subtype-1 neurons were involved in endogenous opioid antinociception. Further neural circuit analysis of the CEA-PB pathway showed that a disinhibitory local circuit within the PB involving GABAergic interneurons and Tacr1-expressing neurons was responsible for mediating the gating of persistent hyperalgesia by $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons. The use of pharmacogenetic and optogenetic manipulations and single-neuron connectome analysis allowed the elucidation of the CEA-PB circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception. Thus, endogenous opioids could inhibit $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which in turn suppress $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB disinhibitory circuits, leading to the alleviation of persistent hyperalgesia by recruiting $\mathrm{PB}^{\mathrm{Tacr1}}$ neurons (Fig. 7).

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] MOR activation in the CEA for endogenous opioid antinociception during persistent hyperalgesia In the present study, we demonstrated the indispensable role of MORs expressed in the CEA in endogenous opioid antinociception in a mouse model of persistent inflammatory hyperalgesia. This was evidenced by the data showing that selective deletion of MORs in the CEA impaired recovery from CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Subcortical projection patterns of bilateral PB relay neurons Another major target region of SPNs is the PB, which is known to receive bilateral spinal projections and to process pain, itch, and touch information. $^{3,11,13,45}$ Although the downstream brain areas of diverse groups of PB neurons have been examined with the bulk-labeling approach, $^{13,46,47}$ the pattern by which PB relay neurons distribute somatosensory information remains largely unknown. We labeled and reconstructed 193 ipsilateral (in right PB) and 67 contralateral (in left PB) PB relay neurons (Figure 4A) and detected dense arborization in the MD, MRN, PAG, LHA, SCm, and CEA (Figure S11A). Given that ipsilateral and contralateral spino-parabrachial pathways are differentially involved in nociceptive signal processing, $^{13}$ we compared the projection patterns of ipsilateral and contralateral PB relay neurons. Although the whole-brain projection patterns of these two groups were largely comparable, we found that ipsilateral PB relay neurons sent more projections to the post-piriform transition area and cortical amygdala area compared with contralateral PB relay neurons (Figures 4B and 4C). This differential downstream innervation pattern indicates differential roles for ipsilateral and contralateral spino-parabrachial pathways. Figure 4. Activation of glutamatergic neurons in the PB is known to induce pain-related behaviors [48]. We hypothesized that an increase in the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons during persistent hyperalgesia may increase the activity of PB glutamatergic neurons via $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB projections; thus, suppressing the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons by endogenous opioids could reduce persistent hyperalgesia. Given that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons are GABAergic [6], we hypothesized that activation of the $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB pathway increases the activity of PB excitatory neurons via a local disinhibitory circuit in the PB. We thus examined the synaptic connectivity between $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons and GABAergic and non-GABAergic neurons in the PB. We generated MOR-iCreER $^{\mathrm{T2}}$ /Gad2-T2a-NLS-mCherry mice, in which ChR2 and mCherry could be expressed in $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons and GABAergic neurons, respectively, via local viral injection (Fig. 6A and B, see Methods). Whole-cell patch-clamp recording was performed on brain slices to measure inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) from GABAergic $(\mathsf{m}\mathsf{Cherry}^{+})$ and non-GABAergic $(\mathsf{m}\mathsf{Cherry}^{-})$ neurons in the PB (Fig. 6A-C).

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] INTRODUCTION Opioids have been used for pain relief for thousands of years and are the most powerful painkillers. Opioid receptors and their ligands are widely expressed in the pain pathway, indicating the potential role of endogenously produced opioid peptides in modulating pain processing [1,2]. The analgesic effect of endogenous opioids has been demonstrated in many pharmacological studies [3-5]. Recent studies have also shown that neurons involved in endogenous opioid analgesia in inflammatory pain are distinct from those involved in exogenous opioids [6]. Thus, in addition to the use of opioid-related analgesic drugs, enhancing endogenous opioid analgesia by targeting endogenous opioid release or the underlying circuits could be an alternative approach to pain management. In this study, we aimed to elu cidate the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception, a type of endogenous analgesia that contributes to the resolution of hyperalgesia and is mediated by the mu-opioid receptor (MOR), which is known to play a dominant role in exogenous and endogenous opioid analgesia [6-8].

question: What supports the idea that the CEA-PB pathway is critical for endogenous opioid antinociception?

We found that endogenous opioid antinociception was mediated by MORs expressed in CEA inhibitory projection neurons. Using single-neuron projectome analysis, we defined the projection subtypes of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, each of which could project to multiple brain regions. Based on the projectome patterns of single $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, we showed that PB-projecting axon branches of subtype-1 neurons were involved in endogenous opioid antinociception. Further neural circuit analysis of the CEA-PB pathway showed that a disinhibitory local circuit within the PB involving GABAergic interneurons and Tacr1-expressing neurons was responsible for mediating the gating of persistent hyperalgesia by $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons. The use of pharmacogenetic and optogenetic manipulations and single-neuron connectome analysis allowed the elucidation of the CEA-PB circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception. Thus, endogenous opioids could inhibit $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which in turn suppress $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB disinhibitory circuits, leading to the alleviation of persistent hyperalgesia by recruiting $\mathrm{PB}^{\mathrm{Tacr1}}$ neurons (Fig. 7).

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] ABSTRACT Endogenous opioid antinociception is a self-regulatory mechanism that reduces chronic pain, but its underlying circuit mechanism remains largely unknown. Here, we showed that endogenous opioid antinociception required the activation of mu-opioid receptors (MORs) in GABAergic neurons of the central amygdala nucleus (CEA) in a persistent-hyperalgesia mouse model. Pharmacogenetic suppression of these $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which mimics the effect of MOR activation, alleviated the persistent hyperalgesia. Furthermore, single-neuron projection analysis revealed multiple projectome-based subtypes of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, each innervating distinct target brain regions. We found that the suppression of axon branches projecting to the parabrachial nucleus (PB) of one subtype of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons alleviated persistent hyperalgesia, indicating a subtype- and axonal-branch-specific mechanism of action. Further electrophysiological analysis revealed that suppression of a distinct CEA-PB disinhibitory circuit controlled endogenous opioid antinociception. Thus, this study identified the central neural circuit that underlies endogenous opioid antinociception, providing new insight into the endogenous pain modulatory mechanisms. Keywords: endogenous opioid antinociception, mu-opioid receptors, central amygdala nucleus, parabrachial nucleus, single-neuron projectome

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] The CEAMOR-PB circuit underlying endogenous antinociception Next, we investigated the local circuit involved in the endogenous modulation of nociception. Activation of glutamatergic neurons in the PB is known to induce pain-related behaviors [48]. We hypothesized that an increase in the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons during persistent hyperalgesia may increase the activity of PB glutamatergic neurons via $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB projections; thus, suppressing the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons by endogenous opioids could reduce persistent hyperalgesia. Given that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons are GABAergic [6], we hypothesized that activation of the $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB pathway increases the activity of PB excitatory neurons via a local disinhibitory circuit in the PB. We thus examined the synaptic connectivity between $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons and GABAergic and non-GABAergic neurons in the PB. We generated MOR-iCreER $^{\mathrm{T2}}$ /Gad2-T2a-NLS-mCherry mice, in which ChR2 and mCherry could be expressed in $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons and GABAergic neurons, respectively, via local viral injection (Fig. 6A and B, see Methods). [source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] INTRODUCTION Opioids have been used for pain relief for thousands of years and are the most powerful painkillers. Opioid receptors and their ligands are widely expressed in the pain pathway, indicating the potential role of endogenously produced opioid peptides in modulating pain processing [1,2]. The analgesic effect of endogenous opioids has been demonstrated in many pharmacological studies [3-5]. Recent studies have also shown that neurons involved in endogenous opioid analgesia in inflammatory pain are distinct from those involved in exogenous opioids [6]. Thus, in addition to the use of opioid-related analgesic drugs, enhancing endogenous opioid analgesia by targeting endogenous opioid release or the underlying circuits could be an alternative approach to pain management. In this study, we aimed to elu cidate the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception, a type of endogenous analgesia that contributes to the resolution of hyperalgesia and is mediated by the mu-opioid receptor (MOR), which is known to play a dominant role in exogenous and endogenous opioid analgesia [6-8].

Since we found that the same suppression induced hyperalgesia, as evidenced by a decrease in the paw withdrawal latency and mechanical nociceptive threshold in response to basal nociceptive sensitivity (Fig. S7P and Q) without significantly affecting locomotion (Fig. S7R), the effect of optogenetic suppression of the projection on CFA-induced hyperalgesia was further determined on CFA d7 and d21, when the hyperalgesia was gradually recovered (Fig. 5M and N). We found that suppression of the $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PAG projection induced a significant decrease in the mechanical nociceptive threshold and paw withdrawal latency (Fig. 5M and N), indicating that this suppression induced hyperalgesia. Additionally, half of subtype-1 $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons projected to the ipsilateral ventral tegmental area (VTA) (Fig. 4F and G, and Fig. S6M), which is known to be involved in pain modulation [45]. We next examined the effect of optogenetically suppressing subtype-1 $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neuron projections in the VTA (Fig. 5O and P), and found that this suppression did not significantly affect the nociceptive threshold during CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia and locomotion (Fig. 5Q and R, and Fig. S7S-U). This result suggests that PB-projecting axon branches of subtype-1 $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons play an essential role in endogenous opioid antinociception. Figure 5.

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] The CEAMOR-PB circuit underlying endogenous antinociception Next, we investigated the local circuit involved in the endogenous modulation of nociception. Activation of glutamatergic neurons in the PB is known to induce pain-related behaviors [48].
