retrieved_docs: [source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] MOR activation in the CEA for endogenous opioid antinociception during persistent hyperalgesia In the present study, we demonstrated the indispensable role of MORs expressed in the CEA in endogenous opioid antinociception in a mouse model of persistent inflammatory hyperalgesia. This was evidenced by the data showing that selective deletion of MORs in the CEA impaired recovery from CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. The important role of MORs expressed in the CEA was further supported by data showing that endogenous opioid antinociception could be largely restored in both male and female MOR-null mice by selectively restoring MOR expression in CEA neurons. Given that similar results were also observed in female mice, the majority of our experiments exclusively utilized male mice, aiming to minimize the use of experimental animals. Our strategy for re-expressing MORs helped to restore the original pattern of MOR expression [6], which is difficult to achieve by transgenic approaches [8,49]. This genetic approach could also discriminate the effects mediated by pre- vs. postsynaptic MORs, which have been difficult to examine by traditional pharmacological approaches. Our results suggest that CEA is important for pain modulation [17,50], and is involved in endogenous opioid analgesia [51,52].

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] Projectome-guided neural circuit analysis As the major output nucleus of the amygdala, the CEA has been extensively studied [65]. Most previous studies on the neural mechanisms of the CEA in different physiological processes (i.e. fear, pain modulation) were mostly based on molecularly defined subtypes of CEA neurons [17,66,67]. Using single-neuron projectome analysis, we demonstrated that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons could be further classified into subtypes based on the distinct patterns of their axon projections. This analysis revealed the structural complexity of molecularly defined neurons, particularly in their branching patterns and preferential projection targets. The information on projectome-based subtypes further guided our dissection of the circuit basis of endogenous opioid antinociception. We found that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons were involved in endogenous opioid antinociception in a subtype-dependent manner. This was evidenced by the finding that optogenetic suppression of axon projections at the major target of subtype-1 but not subtype-2 $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons could alleviate persistent hyperalgesia, mimicking endogenous opioid antinociception. Our projectome analysis showed that the axons of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons exhibited a complex branching pattern targeting multiple brain regions and showed target preferences for each $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ subtype.

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] MOR activation in the CEA for endogenous opioid antinociception during persistent hyperalgesia In the present study, we demonstrated the indispensable role of MORs expressed in the CEA in endogenous opioid antinociception in a mouse model of persistent inflammatory hyperalgesia. This was evidenced by the data showing that selective deletion of MORs in the CEA impaired recovery from CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. The important role of MORs expressed in the CEA was further supported by data showing that endogenous opioid antinociception could be largely restored in both male and female MOR-null mice by selectively restoring MOR expression in CEA neurons. Given that similar results were also observed in female mice, the majority of our experiments exclusively utilized male mice, aiming to minimize the use of experimental animals. Our strategy for re-expressing MORs helped to restore the original pattern of MOR expression [6], which is difficult to achieve by transgenic approaches [8,49]. This genetic approach could also discriminate the effects mediated by pre- vs. postsynaptic MORs, which have been difficult to examine by traditional pharmacological approaches. Our results suggest that CEA is important for pain modulation [17,50], and is involved in endogenous opioid analgesia [51,52].

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] The CEAMOR-PB circuit underlying endogenous antinociception Next, we investigated the local circuit involved in the endogenous modulation of nociception. Activation of glutamatergic neurons in the PB is known to induce pain-related behaviors [48]. We hypothesized that an increase in the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons during persistent hyperalgesia may increase the activity of PB glutamatergic neurons via $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB projections; thus, suppressing the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons by endogenous opioids could reduce persistent hyperalgesia. Given that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons are GABAergic [6], we hypothesized that activation of the $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB pathway increases the activity of PB excitatory neurons via a local disinhibitory circuit in the PB. We thus examined the synaptic connectivity between $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons and GABAergic and non-GABAergic neurons in the PB. We generated MOR-iCreER $^{\mathrm{T2}}$ /Gad2-T2a-NLS-mCherry mice, in which ChR2 and mCherry could be expressed in $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons and GABAergic neurons, respectively, via local viral injection (Fig. 6A and B, see Methods). Whole-cell patch-clamp recording was performed on brain slices to measure inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) from GABAergic $(\mathsf{m}\mathsf{Cherry}^{+})$ and non-GABAergic $(\mathsf{m}\mathsf{Cherry}^{-})$ neurons in the PB (Fig. 6A-C).

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] The amygdala-PB pathway mediates the antinociceptive effect of $\mathsf{CEA}^{\mathsf{MOR}}$ neurons Single-neuron projectome analysis of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons provided the basis for deciphering the circuit mechanism underlying the role of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons in endogenous opioid antinociception. We found that all $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons in projection subtype-1 projected to the PB, a key relay brain region for nociceptive information processing [26,37]. Using whole-cell recording of brain slices, we confirmed that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons provided inhibitory inputs to PB neurons (Fig. S7A–G), which was consistent with previous reports [38,39]. We then tested the involvement of the pathway from subtype-1 $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons to the PB in endogenous opioid antinociception by determining whether suppressing this pathway mimicked the effect of MOR activation in the CEA to alleviate CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. To selectively suppress the synaptic terminals of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons in the PB, we injected the AAV-hSyn-DIO-hM4Di-mCherry virus, or AAV-Ef1α-DIO-EYFP virus as a control, into the right CEA of MOR-iCreERT $^{2/-}$ mice and implanted a cannula above the ipsilateral PB for CNO infusion (Fig. 5A and B).

We demonstrated that subtype-1 $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons were engaged in endogenous opioid antinociception via their axon projections to the PB, which is widely known to be an important central relay for nociceptive information processing [37,68]. This substantiated the notion that the CEA-PB pathway is involved in pain modulation [39,69,70] by identifying the CEA neuron subtype involved in the modulation of endogenous antinociception. Notably, subtype-1 neurons have axon branches that target other brain areas besides PB, such as PAG. Although PAG, as a key component of the descending pain modulatory circuit, has previously been strongly implicated in endogenous analgesia, both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons in the PAG were found receiving GABAergic inputs from CEA [41,43,44]. Our data showed that optogenetic suppression of the projection from $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons to PAG induced thermal and mechanical hyperalgesia and exhibited the opposite role to endogenous opioid antinociceptive effects, which is in line with a recent study [71]. The other major target, VTA, is not involved in endogenous opioid antinociception either. This projectome-guided circuit analysis underscores the importance of addressing distinct functions performed by axon branches of the same type of neuron projecting to different target regions.

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] Projectome-guided neural circuit analysis As the major output nucleus of the amygdala, the CEA has been extensively studied [65]. Most previous studies on the neural mechanisms of the CEA in different physiological processes (i.e. fear, pain modulation) were mostly based on molecularly defined subtypes of CEA neurons [17,66,67]. Using single-neuron projectome analysis, we demonstrated that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons could be further classified into subtypes based on the distinct patterns of their axon projections. This analysis revealed the structural complexity of molecularly defined neurons, particularly in their branching patterns and preferential projection targets. The information on projectome-based subtypes further guided our dissection of the circuit basis of endogenous opioid antinociception. We found that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons were involved in endogenous opioid antinociception in a subtype-dependent manner. This was evidenced by the finding that optogenetic suppression of axon projections at the major target of subtype-1 but not subtype-2 $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons could alleviate persistent hyperalgesia, mimicking endogenous opioid antinociception. Our projectome analysis showed that the axons of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons exhibited a complex branching pattern targeting multiple brain regions and showed target preferences for each $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ subtype.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] We calculated the dissimilarity matrix among all cortical neurons using FNT-dist (Figure 1D; STAR Methods). We found that the three top-level neuron classes (IT, PT, and CT neurons) were well separated (Figure 1D). Within the IT, PT, and CT neurons, the axon morphology is strongly dependent on soma locations across cortical areas and laminar depths (Figure 1E). Using hierarchical clustering, we identified 346 projectome-defined neuron subtypes consisting of 201 IT, 78 PT, and 67 CT subtypes (Figures 1F, 1G, and S2–S4; Table S2). The somata of these subtypes exhibited topographic distribution over the mouse cortex. In each of 43 cortical regions, there are multiple enriched projectome subtypes of IT, PT, and CT neurons (Table S3). As an example, we displayed representative projectome subtypes enriched in SSp-bfd (Figure 1H). Together, we generated a comprehensive dataset of single-neuron projectomes in the whole mouse cortex covering all major types of cortical projection neurons and obtained an unbiased classification of cortical projection neurons.

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] MOR activation in the CEA for endogenous opioid antinociception during persistent hyperalgesia In the present study, we demonstrated the indispensable role of MORs expressed in the CEA in endogenous opioid antinociception in a mouse model of persistent inflammatory hyperalgesia. This was evidenced by the data showing that selective deletion of MORs in the CEA impaired recovery from CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. The important role of MORs expressed in the CEA was further supported by data showing that endogenous opioid antinociception could be largely restored in both male and female MOR-null mice by selectively restoring MOR expression in CEA neurons. Given that similar results were also observed in female mice, the majority of our experiments exclusively utilized male mice, aiming to minimize the use of experimental animals. Our strategy for re-expressing MORs helped to restore the original pattern of MOR expression [6], which is difficult to achieve by transgenic approaches [8,49]. This genetic approach could also discriminate the effects mediated by pre- vs. postsynaptic MORs, which have been difficult to examine by traditional pharmacological approaches. Our results suggest that CEA is important for pain modulation [17,50], and is involved in endogenous opioid analgesia [51,52].

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] The CEAMOR-PB circuit underlying endogenous antinociception Next, we investigated the local circuit involved in the endogenous modulation of nociception. Activation of glutamatergic neurons in the PB is known to induce pain-related behaviors [48]. We hypothesized that an increase in the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons during persistent hyperalgesia may increase the activity of PB glutamatergic neurons via $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB projections; thus, suppressing the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons by endogenous opioids could reduce persistent hyperalgesia. Given that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons are GABAergic [6], we hypothesized that activation of the $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB pathway increases the activity of PB excitatory neurons via a local disinhibitory circuit in the PB. For single-neuron projectome data, Supplementary Fig. 1a shows the procedure for sample exclusion. In brief, investigators were blinded to the identity of the brain samples being processed. Brain samples with excessively dense labeling, which precludes single-axon tracing, were excluded from subsequent neuronal tracing procedures. All traced neurons underwent multiple rounds of manual verification to ensure accuracy. Neurons with erroneous tracing data were excluded from further analysis. Additionally, neurons with soma locations outside the hypothalamus were excluded unless otherwise stated. All other neurons included for analysis in the present study had explicitly stated identifiers (for example, soma location, neuropeptide population or target regions). For EASI-FISH experiments, brain slices from two independently injected male mice (biological replicates) were processed for imaging and grouped for analysis, following the standard protocol for single-neuron analysis. For all other histological studies, at least three biological replicates were obtained for each experiment. For a detailed summary of the statistical analysis, see Supplementary Table 6.

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] The CEAMOR-PB circuit underlying endogenous antinociception Next, we investigated the local circuit involved in the endogenous modulation of nociception. Activation of glutamatergic neurons in the PB is known to induce pain-related behaviors [48]. We hypothesized that an increase in the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons during persistent hyperalgesia may increase the activity of PB glutamatergic neurons via $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB projections; thus, suppressing the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons by endogenous opioids could reduce persistent hyperalgesia. Given that $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons are GABAergic [6], we hypothesized that activation of the $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB pathway increases the activity of PB excitatory neurons via a local disinhibitory circuit in the PB. We thus examined the synaptic connectivity between $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons and GABAergic and non-GABAergic neurons in the PB. We generated MOR-iCreER $^{\mathrm{T2}}$ /Gad2-T2a-NLS-mCherry mice, in which ChR2 and mCherry could be expressed in $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons and GABAergic neurons, respectively, via local viral injection (Fig. 6A and B, see Methods). Whole-cell patch-clamp recording was performed on brain slices to measure inhibitory postsynaptic currents (IPSCs) from GABAergic $(\mathsf{m}\mathsf{Cherry}^{+})$ and non-GABAergic $(\mathsf{m}\mathsf{Cherry}^{-})$ neurons in the PB (Fig. 6A-C).

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] Limitations In the current study, due to different purposes, the experiments were performed on different days after CFA injection. CFA-induced hyperalgesia was characterized by a change in nociceptive sensitivity. After CFA injection, mice would exhibit hyperalgesia, followed by slow recovery to nearly basal level 3-4 weeks later. This recovery was shown to be mediated by endogenous activation of MORs [6,13,51]. Thus, most of the behavioral tests examining the effect of different manipulation on recovery of hyperalgesia were performed across the 49 days of the experiment. However, this does not apply to the experiments in Fig. 3A-D and Fig. 5, whose aim was to mimic the MOR-mediated endogenous opioid antinociception by pharmacogenetic or optogenetic suppression of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons or the CEA-PB circuit. These manipulations could only be performed in the early days but not at a later stage, when the hyperalgesia had already recovered to basal level. For the prolonged pharmacogenetic activation of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, CNO was injected every other day, and the behavioral test was terminated at day 21 after CFA injection, when the hyperalgesia largely recovered (Fig. 3H and I). For testing the effect of MOR antagonists in blocking the endogenous opioid activation, we tested the effect of different antagonists at late stages, when the endogenous opioid system was activated (Fig. 1S, V and W).

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] Increased excitability of $\mathsf{CEA}^{\mathsf{MOR}}$ neurons during CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia The involvement of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which are widely distributed in the lateral (CEAl), capsular (CEAc) and medial (CEAm) subdivisions of the amygdala (Fig. S2, Movies S1 and S2), in the inflammatory hyperalgesia was further examined by measuring the activity of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons with in vivo fiber photometry. The fluorescent $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ probe GCaMP6s was expressed specifically in $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons by injecting AAV-hSyn-DIO-GCaMP6s into the right CEA of MOR-iCreER $^{\mathrm{T2+/--}}$ mice, and optical fibers were implanted above the injection site (Fig. 2A and B). One month after viral injection, the response of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons in the right CEA to right but not left hindpaw pinch (noxious mechanical stimulus) was markedly increased after intraplantar CFA injection compared with the responses in the same group of mice before CFA treatment (Fig. 2C-H). We further analyzed the location of the tip of optical fibers in the CEA subregions, and found that the signal we collected was mainly from the population in the CEAm and CEAl (Fig. S3A and B). These results indicate that the excitability of a specific group of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons was greatly increased during persistent hyperalgesia induced by CFA injection, consistent with that observed during chronic pain induced by nerve injury [17]. Notably, we found that 'late-firing' $\mathrm{CEA^{\mathrm{MOR}}}$ neurons in CFA-treated mice exhibited a significantly increased firing rate (Fig. 2L and M) and reduced rheobase (Fig. 2N) compared to those of saline-treated mice. In contrast, the physiological properties of $\mathrm{CEA^{\mathrm{MOR}}}$ neurons with two other firing patterns did not exhibit significant differences between the two groups (Fig. S3H-S). Thus, the intrinsic excitability of the 'late-firing' $\mathrm{CEA^{\mathrm{MOR}}}$ neurons was selectively increased in CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. To further investigate the involvement of 'late-firing' $\mathrm{CEA^{\mathrm{MOR}}}$ neurons in CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia, we measured the excitability of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons 3 weeks after CFA injection when the mice had recovered from persistent hyperalgesia (Fig. 2P and Q). We found that the firing rate of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons in the CFA-injected group was significantly decreased (Fig. 2R), and there was no significant difference in the rheobase (Fig. 2S) compared to that of saline-treated mice. We next examined whether activation of the opioid system is involved in the recovery of excitability in $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons.

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] Limitations In the current study, due to different purposes, the experiments were performed on different days after CFA injection. CFA-induced hyperalgesia was characterized by a change in nociceptive sensitivity. After CFA injection, mice would exhibit hyperalgesia, followed by slow recovery to nearly basal level 3-4 weeks later. This recovery was shown to be mediated by endogenous activation of MORs [6,13,51]. Thus, most of the behavioral tests examining the effect of different manipulation on recovery of hyperalgesia were performed across the 49 days of the experiment. However, this does not apply to the experiments in Fig. 3A-D and Fig. 5, whose aim was to mimic the MOR-mediated endogenous opioid antinociception by pharmacogenetic or optogenetic suppression of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons or the CEA-PB circuit. These manipulations could only be performed in the early days but not at a later stage, when the hyperalgesia had already recovered to basal level. For the prolonged pharmacogenetic activation of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, CNO was injected every other day, and the behavioral test was terminated at day 21 after CFA injection, when the hyperalgesia largely recovered (Fig. 3H and I). For testing the effect of MOR antagonists in blocking the endogenous opioid activation, we tested the effect of different antagonists at late stages, when the endogenous opioid system was activated (Fig. 1S, V and W).
answer: Pharmacogenetic suppression of PBTacr1 neurons alleviated CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia without affecting locomotor activity.

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] MOR activation in the CEA for endogenous opioid antinociception during persistent hyperalgesia In the present study, we demonstrated the indispensable role of MORs expressed in the CEA in endogenous opioid antinociception in a mouse model of persistent inflammatory hyperalgesia. This was evidenced by the data showing that selective deletion of MORs in the CEA impaired recovery from CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. The important role of MORs expressed in the CEA was further supported by data showing that endogenous opioid antinociception could be largely restored in both male and female MOR-null mice by selectively restoring MOR expression in CEA neurons. Given that similar results were also observed in female mice, the majority of our experiments exclusively utilized male mice, aiming to minimize the use of experimental animals. Our strategy for re-expressing MORs helped to restore the original pattern of MOR expression [6], which is difficult to achieve by transgenic approaches [8,49]. This genetic approach could also discriminate the effects mediated by pre- vs. postsynaptic MORs, which have been difficult to examine by traditional pharmacological approaches. Our results suggest that CEA is important for pain modulation [17,50], and is involved in endogenous opioid analgesia [51,52].

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] ABSTRACT Endogenous opioid antinociception is a self-regulatory mechanism that reduces chronic pain, but its underlying circuit mechanism remains largely unknown. Here, we showed that endogenous opioid antinociception required the activation of mu-opioid receptors (MORs) in GABAergic neurons of the central amygdala nucleus (CEA) in a persistent-hyperalgesia mouse model. Pharmacogenetic suppression of these $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which mimics the effect of MOR activation, alleviated the persistent hyperalgesia. Furthermore, single-neuron projection analysis revealed multiple projectome-based subtypes of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, each innervating distinct target brain regions. We found that the suppression of axon branches projecting to the parabrachial nucleus (PB) of one subtype of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons alleviated persistent hyperalgesia, indicating a subtype- and axonal-branch-specific mechanism of action. Further electrophysiological analysis revealed that suppression of a distinct CEA-PB disinhibitory circuit controlled endogenous opioid antinociception. Thus, this study identified the central neural circuit that underlies endogenous opioid antinociception, providing new insight into the endogenous pain modulatory mechanisms. Keywords: endogenous opioid antinociception, mu-opioid receptors, central amygdala nucleus, parabrachial nucleus, single-neuron projectome

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] DISCUSSION In this study, we identified a neural circuit that was essential for mediating endogenous opioid antinociception during CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. We found that endogenous opioid antinociception was mediated by MORs expressed in CEA inhibitory projection neurons. Using single-neuron projectome analysis, we defined the projection subtypes of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, each of which could project to multiple brain regions. Based on the projectome patterns of single $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, we showed that PB-projecting axon branches of subtype-1 neurons were involved in endogenous opioid antinociception. Further neural circuit analysis of the CEA-PB pathway showed that a disinhibitory local circuit within the PB involving GABAergic interneurons and Tacr1-expressing neurons was responsible for mediating the gating of persistent hyperalgesia by $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons. The use of pharmacogenetic and optogenetic manipulations and single-neuron connectome analysis allowed the elucidation of the CEA-PB circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception. Thus, endogenous opioids could inhibit $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which in turn suppress $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB disinhibitory circuits, leading to the alleviation of persistent hyperalgesia by recruiting $\mathrm{PB}^{\mathrm{Tacr1}}$ neurons (Fig. 7).

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] DISCUSSION In this study, we identified a neural circuit that was essential for mediating endogenous opioid antinociception during CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. [source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] ABSTRACT Endogenous opioid antinociception is a self-regulatory mechanism that reduces chronic pain, but its underlying circuit mechanism remains largely unknown. Here, we showed that endogenous opioid antinociception required the activation of mu-opioid receptors (MORs) in GABAergic neurons of the central amygdala nucleus (CEA) in a persistent-hyperalgesia mouse model. Pharmacogenetic suppression of these $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which mimics the effect of MOR activation, alleviated the persistent hyperalgesia. Furthermore, single-neuron projection analysis revealed multiple projectome-based subtypes of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, each innervating distinct target brain regions. We found that the suppression of axon branches projecting to the parabrachial nucleus (PB) of one subtype of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons alleviated persistent hyperalgesia, indicating a subtype- and axonal-branch-specific mechanism of action. Further electrophysiological analysis revealed that suppression of a distinct CEA-PB disinhibitory circuit controlled endogenous opioid antinociception. Thus, this study identified the central neural circuit that underlies endogenous opioid antinociception, providing new insight into the endogenous pain modulatory mechanisms. [source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] DISCUSSION In this study, we identified a neural circuit that was essential for mediating endogenous opioid antinociception during CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. Using single-neuron projectome analysis, we defined the projection subtypes of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, each of which could project to multiple brain regions. Based on the projectome patterns of single $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, we showed that PB-projecting axon branches of subtype-1 neurons were involved in endogenous opioid antinociception. Further neural circuit analysis of the CEA-PB pathway showed that a disinhibitory local circuit within the PB involving GABAergic interneurons and Tacr1-expressing neurons was responsible for mediating the gating of persistent hyperalgesia by $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons. The use of pharmacogenetic and optogenetic manipulations and single-neuron connectome analysis allowed the elucidation of the CEA-PB circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception. Thus, endogenous opioids could inhibit $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which in turn suppress $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ -PB disinhibitory circuits, leading to the alleviation of persistent hyperalgesia by recruiting $\mathrm{PB}^{\mathrm{Tacr1}}$ neurons (Fig. 7).

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] MOR activation in the CEA for endogenous opioid antinociception during persistent hyperalgesia In the present study, we demonstrated the indispensable role of MORs expressed in the CEA in endogenous opioid antinociception in a mouse model of persistent inflammatory hyperalgesia. This was evidenced by the data showing that selective deletion of MORs in the CEA impaired recovery from CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. The important role of MORs expressed in the CEA was further supported by data showing that endogenous opioid antinociception could be largely restored in both male and female MOR-null mice by selectively restoring MOR expression in CEA neurons. This genetic approach could also discriminate the effects mediated by pre- vs. postsynaptic MORs, which have been difficult to examine by traditional pharmacological approaches. Our results suggest that CEA is important for pain modulation [17,50], and is involved in endogenous opioid analgesia [51,52].

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] INTRODUCTION Opioids have been used for pain relief for thousands of years and are the most powerful painkillers. Opioid receptors and their ligands are widely expressed in the pain pathway, indicating the potential role of endogenously produced opioid peptides in modulating pain processing [1,2]. The analgesic effect of endogenous opioids has been demonstrated in many pharmacological studies [3-5]. Recent studies have also shown that neurons involved in endogenous opioid analgesia in inflammatory pain are distinct from those involved in exogenous opioids [6]. Thus, in addition to the use of opioid-related analgesic drugs, enhancing endogenous opioid analgesia by targeting endogenous opioid release or the underlying circuits could be an alternative approach to pain management. In this study, we aimed to elu cidate the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception, a type of endogenous analgesia that contributes to the resolution of hyperalgesia and is mediated by the mu-opioid receptor (MOR), which is known to play a dominant role in exogenous and endogenous opioid analgesia [6-8].

[source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] DISCUSSION In this study, we identified a neural circuit that was essential for mediating endogenous opioid antinociception during CFA-induced persistent hyperalgesia. [source: Dou et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectome-guided analysis reveals the neural circuit mechanism underlying endogenous opioid antinociception.md] ABSTRACT Endogenous opioid antinociception is a self-regulatory mechanism that reduces chronic pain, but its underlying circuit mechanism remains largely unknown. Here, we showed that endogenous opioid antinociception required the activation of mu-opioid receptors (MORs) in GABAergic neurons of the central amygdala nucleus (CEA) in a persistent-hyperalgesia mouse model. Pharmacogenetic suppression of these $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, which mimics the effect of MOR activation, alleviated the persistent hyperalgesia. Furthermore, single-neuron projection analysis revealed multiple projectome-based subtypes of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons, each innervating distinct target brain regions. We found that the suppression of axon branches projecting to the parabrachial nucleus (PB) of one subtype of $\mathrm{CEA}^{\mathrm{MOR}}$ neurons alleviated persistent hyperalgesia, indicating a subtype- and axonal-branch-specific mechanism of action. Further electrophysiological analysis revealed that suppression of a distinct CEA-PB disinhibitory circuit controlled endogenous opioid antinociception. Thus, this study identified the central neural circuit that underlies endogenous opioid antinociception, providing new insight into the endogenous pain modulatory mechanisms. We identified distinct groups of projectome subtypes projecting to each of the four cortico-cortical subnetworks. Interestingly, projectome analysis showed that the segregation of first-order axon collaterals can define different subnetworks. Further analysis also revealed that the somata of each subtype are distributed with specific topography within PFC; that the collateral branch location on the primary axon correlates with the proximity of the target; and that the distribution of axon terminal arbors at the target divides the target into subdomains. Taken together, this work provides a comprehensive resource for mouse PFC projectomes at the single-neuron level and demonstrates how this resource could be used to reveal organizing principles of whole-brain PFC projections.

We found that the axon terminals of IT neurons are of longer length and larger volume than those of PT neurons (Figures 4K and S9A). Using the same approach for the subdivision of SNr, we obtained 14 discrete striatal subdomains (Figures 4L and S9B; STAR Methods). Compared with the subdivisions of striatum previously identified by Hintiryan et al.30 and Foster et al.,29 we found that although the exact numbers of subdivisions were different ( $n = 3 0$ in Hintiryan et al.30 vs. $n = 1 4$ in this study), their spatial configurations were largely consistent (Figures S9C–S9E). Our topographic projection pattern was also similar to that in non-human primates,33 indicating a conserved feature of cortico-striatal projection. Moreover, we found highly consistent organizations of cortico-striatal projections for IT and PT neurons (Figures 4M, S9F, S9G, and S9H). Furthermore, we also observed convergent projections to striatal subdomains from different cortical areas. We next aligned the axons of all PFC projection neurons and calculated the pairwise dissimilarity score of their axon morphology using a rigorous dynamic programming algorithm, FNT-dist (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Method 2). These neurons were then clustered by unsupervised hierarchical clustering (Fig. 1e and Methods). Among all PFC neurons we analyzed, IT neurons are the most abundant (3,744) and can be divided into ipsilaterally projecting only (IT-ipsi) and contralaterally projecting (IT-contra) neurons, followed by PT (1,528) and CT neurons (1,085). Comparing our single-neuron projectome dataset with previous bulk labeling results in matched spatial locations, the whole-brain projections of combined single-neuron projectomes and bulk labeling experiments are significantly similar (0.9, Pearson's correlation coefficient), indicating that single-neuron projectomes recapitulated the bulk labeling results (Extended Data Fig. 2b). Based on the clustering analysis, we further classified IT, PT and CT neurons into a total of 64 subtypes (44 for IT, 12 for PT and 8 for CT) (Fig. 1e). question: What algorithm was used to calculate the pairwise dissimilarity of axon morphology among PFC neurons?
retrieved_docs: [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] We first simplified the axon morphology of single neurons using farthest point sampling and FNT-decimate to keep the global morphology of neurons. Then, we computed the dissimilarity among all neurons using FNT-dist and obtained the dissimilarity matrix. We applied hierarchical clustering to the dissimilarity matrix of IT, PT, and CT neurons, respectively. The numbers of projectome subtypes were determined by calculating the C-index at each number of clusters, from 2 to 300. The dendrograms of IT, PT, and CT neurons were merged based on the mean dissimilarity among them. To examine the low-dimensional organization of single-neuron projectomes, we applied t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) to the dissimilarity matrix using R package Rtsne. The constellation plot was constructed by the get_knn_graph and plot.constellation function in R package scrattch.hicat. We used the R package nat60 to plot the morphology of single neurons and render meshes of brain regions.

[source: Gao et al - 2022 - Single-neuron projectome of mouse prefrontal cortex.md] Discussion The organization of the neural network is likely to be designed for efficient signal processing under the constraint of the limited physical space available within the brain. Critical aspects of this organization include the appropriate strategic spatial distribution of neuronal somata, the arrangement of axons within the fiber tract, the collateral branch patterns relative to their target locations and the tiling of axon terminal arbors within the target areas to achieve wiring specificity as well as economy. In our study, we found that most projectome subtypes reside in selected areas rather than across all PFC areas. First-order axon collateral branch point location is correlated with axon target selection, and the spatial organization of terminal arbor domains of projectome subtypes demarcate the subdivisions of a target structure. It is worth noticing that our unbiased clustering method using FNT-dist based on whole-axon morphology yielded consistent but different results from those based on pre-defined targets, such as cortical subnetworks. It is still unclear which method serves as a better criterion for subtype classification. Furthermore, the functional importance of three distinct PFC modules with strong intra-module recurrent connectivity remains to be further examined. Finally, our finding of one-to-many relationship between transcriptome and projectome subtypes supports the notion that single-cell projectome analysis should be considered together with scRNA-seq analysis to refine PFC subtype definition.

In addition to cortico-cortical projections, PFC IT neurons also project extensively to subcortical targets such as basolateral amygdala (BLA) involved in innate fear response $^{30}$ , dorsal striatum (CP) involved in operant responding $^{31}$ , ventral striatum (ACB) involved in social and flexible behaviors $^{32,33}$ , claustrum (CLA) involved in action control $^{34}$ and pallidum (PAL) involved in reward processing $^{35}$. [source: Gao et al - 2022 - Single-neuron projectome of mouse prefrontal cortex.md] Discussion The organization of the neural network is likely to be designed for efficient signal processing under the constraint of the limited physical space available within the brain. Critical aspects of this organization include the appropriate strategic spatial distribution of neuronal somata, the arrangement of axons within the fiber tract, the collateral branch patterns relative to their target locations and the tiling of axon terminal arbors within the target areas to achieve wiring specificity as well as economy. In our study, we found that most projectome subtypes reside in selected areas rather than across all PFC areas. First-order axon collateral branch point location is correlated with axon target selection, and the spatial organization of terminal arbor domains of projectome subtypes demarcate the subdivisions of a target structure. It is worth noticing that our unbiased clustering method using FNT-dist based on whole-axon morphology yielded consistent but different results from those based on pre-defined targets, such as cortical subnetworks. It is still unclear which method serves as a better criterion for subtype classification. Furthermore, the functional importance of three distinct PFC modules with strong intra-module recurrent connectivity remains to be further examined. Finally, our finding of one-to-many relationship between transcriptome and projectome subtypes supports the notion that single-cell projectome analysis should be considered together with scRNA-seq analysis to refine PFC subtype definition.

[source: Li et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectomes of mouse paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus oxytocin neurons reveal mutually exclusive projection patterns.md] Single-neuron reconstruction of axons, dendrites and somata Single cell axonal projections were manually reconstructed from three sparsely and brightly labeled samples, aided by the FNT software.[25] Full axonal arbors of 115 neurons from sample 18696 (lactating female), 65 neurons from sample 195037 (virgin female) and 84 neurons from sample 195038 (virgin female) were traced. To ensure accurate reconstruction, all axonal arbors were traced by two independent experienced tracers ( $>3$ months of tracing experience); reconstructed results were then merged and examined by another experienced tracer. A previous study, which used the same FNT software, examined tracing quality using quantitative measurements and showed that experienced tracers generated very similar reconstructions, and that accuracy was further increased by merging.[25] Tracing starting points were bright terminals outside of the PVH, to avoid bias in soma positioning; all brightly labeled neurons were traced. As shown in Videos S1 and S2, tracing was done using $0.35 \times 0.35 \times 1.0 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$ high resolution image datasets. The FNT software subdivided datasets into cubes ( $89.6 \times 89.6 \times 100 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$ ), and automatically loaded the next cube to be traced. At this resolution, axons can be easily distinguished from each other. Occasionally, when an axon tangled with another fiber near the soma, we traced both fibers and usually resolved the issue; occasionally, tracing was abandoned because axons could not be traced back to the soma.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] fMOST imaging and neurite tracing The fMOST imaging, neurite tracing, and quality control were conducted as previously described.10 We validated that labeled neurons were largely confined to the intended viral injection sites in the cortex from the inspection of imaging results (Figure S1D). The raw fMOST images were divided into cubes and loaded into Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT) dynamically based on user demand. Two tracers used FNT to reconstruct the morphology of single neurons independently. Then a third tracer proofread their results and obtained the final single neurons of a high quality. During the neurite tracing, neurons with weak signals were discarded and neurons located outside of cortex were not reconstructed.

[source: Gao et al - 2022 - Single-neuron projectome of mouse prefrontal cortex.md] jects to multiple specific targets requires reconstruction of the projection pattern of single sparsely labeled neurons. Such single-neuron projectome analysis for PFC neurons, at a scale comparable to scRNA-seq, is required for a more comprehensive understanding of the diversity of neuron subtypes and the organization principle of their projectomes. However, whole-brain tracing of large numbers of single-neuron projectomes based on terabyte (TB) imaging data poses a formidable challenge. The PFC is the center of high-level cognitive functions, including decision-making $^{11,12}$ , working memory $^{13,14}$ , emotion $^{15,16}$ , attention $^{15,17}$ and perception $^{18,19}$ and is implicated in many neuropsychiatric diseases $^{20}$. Whole-brain connectivity based on bulk labeling of neuronal populations has shown that mouse PFC has extensive connections to nearly all brain areas $^{6}$. More precise long-range projection patterns of individual neurons will provide further functional specificity of diverse subtypes of PFC neurons $^{21,22}$. Although the hierarchical relationship between PFC and other cortical regions has been recently characterized $^{6}$ , the hierarchical ordering of subregions within PFC remains to be clarified. Thus, systematic characterization of PFC single-neuron projectome is critical for elucidating precise connectivity both within and outside PFC. In this study, we developed a software package, Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT), for high-throughput projectome reconstruction and analysis for TB-sized light microscopic imaging data.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] TB-sized CH1 images were processed into one million data cubes with $256 \times 256 \times 90$ voxels using the FNT-slice2cube program of the Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT) software.[26] Cubes used for projectome reconstruction were then compressed with the high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) method. The raw data was down-sampled to the resolution of $20 \times 20 \times 20\mu \mathrm{m}^3$ for the overview of the whole-brain data. FNT was used for reconstruction of the full morphology of neurons as described previously.[26,71] During tracing, the cube that users selected was loaded into the computer memory automatically and visualized in 3D by maximal intensity projection algorithm. FNT tracing process is semi-automatic: 1) a putative path can be found by A-star algorithm only with a starting position; 2) the human tracers will confirm and make revision manually. All neurons were reconstructed by two independent experienced tracers; then these two reconstructed results were merged and examined by another experienced person to obtain the final results. In our tracing process, only neurons with tracing score higher than 90 were included for further analysis. The neuron tracing score was calculated based on the protocols published previously.[26]

To accommodate the experimental data with multi-color imaging, such as PI staining in fMOST technology, FNT allows up to three sets of selected imaging data channels to be visualized at the same time.

An axon projection can be traversed in this way until completion. Different neurons in the same sample were traced by different personnel in parallel and cross-validated after completion. In addition, each traced neuron was independently checked by another person to ensure accuracy, and each brain sample was subjected to random post-tracing quality checks. Registration. The whole brain with information from all reconstructed neurons was registered into the standard Allen CCFv3 (ref. 27) using a previously described method[26]. In brief, we segmented several brain regions as landmarks through cytoarchitecture references. We performed diffeomorphic transformation and symmetric image normalization in Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs) to acquire transformation parameters based on these landmarks. These transformation parameters were applied to all the traced neurons within the brain sample to remap the reconstructed neuron onto the Allen brain template.

question: What is the typical size of a raw EGFP image and how does FNT make this data manageable on a personal computer?
retrieved_docs: [source: Li et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectomes of mouse paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus oxytocin neurons reveal mutually exclusive projection patterns.md] Whole-brain images of sparse labeling samples were acquired using fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography (fMOST) technology. The raw image dataset of each sample includes two channels: the GFP channel (channel 1, CH1) contains morphological information of labeled neurons, while the propidium iodide (PI) channel (channel 2, CH2) contains cytoarchitectonic information. Each dataset has approximately 10000 raw images of $30000 \times 20000$ pixels of both CH1 and CH2, with a voxel resolution of $0.35 \times 0.35 \times 1.0 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$. The coordinate system of raw images is kept consistent in all subsequent processing. The X, Y and Z values of coordinates increased in value along the right-left (X), dorsal-ventral (Y) and anterior-posterior (Z) directions. TB-sized CH1 raw images were divided into one million data cubes of $256 \times 256 \times 100$ voxels using the FNT-slice2cube command of the Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT) software,[25] compressed using the high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) method for reconstruction. CH1 images were downsampled to a resolution of $20 \times 20 \times 20 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$ in the whole-brain projection overview to facilitate identification of the reconstruction start point.

answer: The typical size of a raw EGFP image is approximately 10,000 images of $30,000 \times 20,000$ pixels with a voxel resolution of $0.35 \times 0.35 \times 1.0 \mu m^3$. FNT makes this data manageable by dividing it into one million data cubes of $256 \times 256 \times 100$ voxels and compressing them using the HEVC method.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Sparse labeling of central relay neurons To achieve sparse labeling of central relay neurons in the brain, we injected AAV2/1-CMV-bGI-Cre-EGFP-pA virus (Taitool Inc., titer: 1 x $10^{13}$ v.g./mL) into the spinal dorsal horn with the volume of 20-200 nL (according to the projection strengths). After 1 week, the AAV2/9-EF1a-DIO-EYFP-WPRE-pA virus (Taitool Inc., titer: 1 x $10^{13}$ v.g./mL) was injected into the target brain areas (Detailed information is listed in Table S2).

[source: Jiao et al - 2025 - Projectome-based characterization of hypothalamic peptidergic neurons in male mice.md] Virus We used various methods to achieve sparse labeling of neurons with cell type specificity. For virus injected into Cre animals, these methods included diluting AAVs expressing Cre-dependent GFPs of different versions or mixing AAVs expressing Cre-dependent FlpO and AAVs expressing FlpO-dependent fluorescent protein at a ratio. Viral mixing was achieved by either combining two AAVs produced separately or by co-transfection of mixed plasmid backbones for both AAVs to cells during the viral production step as described[63]. In addition, to label Orexin neurons, we injected AAVs encoding mNeoGreen under the control of the Orexin promoter (PPORX) into wild-type males. Several viruses were used in this study. AAV-CAG-DIO-FlpO (titer, $5.0 \times 10^{9}$ genomic copies per milliliter $(\mathrm{gc} \mathrm{ml}^{-1})$ ) was purchased from Shanghai Taitool Bioscience Co., Ltd. The JS series of virus was a mixture of AAV-hSyn Con/Fon EYFP and AAV-EF1a-FlpO generated at a different ratio during the virus-packaging step (1:4,000, titer, $5.2 \times 10^{12} \mathrm{gc} \mathrm{ml}^{-1}$ ; 1:8,000, titer, $1.41 \times 10^{13} \mathrm{gc} \mathrm{ml}^{-1}$ ; 1:40,000, titer, $5.1 \times 10^{12} \mathrm{gc} \mathrm{ml}^{-1}$ ) which were purchased from Brain Case (Shenzhen) Biotechnology Co., Ltd.

Mice were anesthetized with $2\%$ isoflurance during surgery. Injections were performed using a microsyringe pump (MO-10, Narashige, 13012). Virus was injected by using a pulled-glass pipette of $20\sim 25 - \mu \mathrm{m}$ inside diameter at the tip (Wiretrol II Capillary Microdispenser, Drummond Scientific, 5000-2010). A flaming/brown micropipette puller (Sutter Instrument, P-97) could pull the pipette. The injection pipette went into the brain using a Sutter MPC-220 micromanipulator. We injected AAV2/9-hSyn-EGFP-WPRE-pA (titer: $\sim 10^{13}$ genomes per milliliter; Shanghai Taitool Bioscience) into L2/3 of orbital area, ventrolateral part (ORBvl) and AAV2/9-hSyn-mCherry-WPRE-pA (titer: $\sim 10^{13}$ genomes per milliliter; Shanghai Taitool Bioscience) into L2/3 of anterior cingulate area (ACA) slowly ( $\sim 60\mathrm{nl}$ over $\sim 10$ minutes). After pumping, the pipette stayed for at least 15 minutes to avoid virus spilling to other regions. After 4 weeks, we euthanized the mice and sectioned the whole brain in sagittal plane. For retrograde tracing, the procedure for animal preparation was similar to the anterograde tracing experiment described above.

One week after the injection, another AAV2/9-hEF1a-DIO-EYFP-WPRE-pA virus (Taitool Inc., titer: 1 x $10^{13}$ v.g./mL) was further injected into C1-C4 of spinal dorsal horn (Detailed information is listed in Table S2).

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] The surgery was performed following the protocols published previously.13 Briefly, mice were anesthetized with the mixture of Zoletil (Tiletamine hydrochloride: 15 mg/kg; Zalazepam hydrochloride: 15 mg/kg; purchased from Virbac S.A) and Xylazine hydrochloride (80 mg/kg, purchased from Huamu Veterinary Medicine Co., Ltd.). For intra-brain virus injection, the skull was exposed by midline scalp incision, and craniotomy ( $\sim 1.5$ mm diameter) was made using a hand-held drill for the introduction of microinjection glass pipette according to the coordinates of target brain regions. Viruses were injected into target brain areas at the rate of $\sim 20\mathrm{nL / min}$ using an air-pressure system (Picospritzer III, Parker) or oil-pressure system (Narishige Scientific Instrument Lab). After the completion of virus injection, the glass pipette was left in place for $\sim 5$ min and then withdrew slowly to avoid back-flow of virus. After that, we sutured the skin and put animals on a heating blanket before returning them back to their home cages. For intra-spinal cord virus injection, vertebrae of mice were exposed at C1-C4 and fixed on the stereotaxic frame. For exposure of the spinal cord, the dura was incised using the anatomy needle. A microinjection glass pipette was induced to the spinal dorsal horn with the degree of 30. Virus was delivered into the dorsal spinal cord at the rate of $\sim 10\mathrm{~nL/min}$.

In the neocortex, long-range projection neurons are broadly divided into three classes: intratelencephalic (IT) neurons, pyramidal tract (PT) neurons and corticothalamic (CT) neurons $^{1,2}$. Mesoscopic projections of the mouse at the level of neuron populations have been obtained by using virus-based tracing $^{3,4}$ and neuron-class-specific Cre lines $^{5,6}$. Several recent studies based on single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) showed that transcriptome-defined subtypes within the three broadly defined neuron classes are highly diverse and vary greatly across cortical regions $^{7-9}$. On the other hand, retrograde labeling and scRNA-seq revealed a many-to-many correspondence between transcriptome subtypes of medial PFC neurons and their projection targets $^{10}$. However, to determine whether a single PFC neuron projects to multiple specific targets requires reconstruction of the projection pattern of single sparsely labeled neurons.

question: What process ensures the quality of traced neurons before they are used in the analysis?
retrieved_docs: [source: Gao et al - 2022 - Single-neuron projectome of mouse prefrontal cortex.md] ng in fMOST technology, FNT allows up to three sets of selected imaging data channels to be visualized at the same time. Categorical data, such as brain annotation from the ABA, can also be incorporated. After loading the brain annotation file, the brain area annotation at any chosen position in the brain can be indicated. FNT tracing process consists of three steps: finding a putative path, examining the putative path and extending the current neurite tree, as summarized in Extended Data Fig. 1b. In FNT, we included a new operation: finding a putative path only with a starting position. In FNT, users' confirmation at each step ensures the correctness of tracing. After users confirm that a branch is traced to the end, the branch is marked as finished. FNT keeps the records of all unfinished branches and will automatically jump to the nearest unfinished branch when the current branch is finished. A neuron tree can be traversed in this way until it is completed. Users can easily edit existing branches or un-do previous unwanted operations. A demonstration of FNT tracing process is shown in Supplementary Video 1. Quality control and evaluation. To ensure the validity of tracing result, every neuron was traced by two independent human tracers. Then, the results were merged by a third human tracer. We designed a scoring scheme combining different types of errors to evaluate the quality of tracing result.

All neurons were reconstructed by two independent experienced tracers; then these two reconstructed results were merged and examined by another experienced person to obtain the final results. To ensure accurate reconstruction, all axonal arbors were traced by two independent experienced tracers ( $>3$ months of tracing experience); reconstructed results were then merged and examined by another experienced tracer. A previous study, which used the same FNT software, examined tracing quality using quantitative measurements and showed that experienced tracers generated very similar reconstructions, and that accuracy was further increased by merging.[25] Tracing starting points were bright terminals outside of the PVH, to avoid bias in soma positioning; all brightly labeled neurons were traced. The FNT software subdivided datasets into cubes ( $89.6 \times 89.6 \times 100 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$ ), and automatically loaded the next cube to be traced. At this resolution, axons can be easily distinguished from each other. Occasionally, when an axon tangled with another fiber near the soma, we traced both fibers and usually resolved the issue; occasionally, tracing was abandoned because axons could not be traced back to the soma.

Within the IT, PT, and CT neurons, the axon morphology is strongly dependent on soma locations across cortical areas and laminar depths (Figure 1E). [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] Limitations of the study There are several limitations in our study. First, our dataset is still limited in the number of reconstructed neurons, as it covers a small fraction of actual cortical projection neurons in the mouse brain. The current strategy of sparse sampling may obscure the rare subtypes. More sophisticated intersectional strategies could improve the coverage of projection neurons. Second, the reproducibility of these projectome subtypes of cortical neurons is an important issue. Our definition of neuron subtypes still needs to be cross-validated with other methods.46 Third, for cortico-subcortical projections, although we mapped the finegrained projections from the cortex, these subcortical targets also receive inputs from the brain regions other than cortex. For example, striatum also receives inputs from thalamus. Therefore, a complete description of neural network is still lacking. Fourth, our definition of neuron subtypes was based mostly on the neuron morphologies. However, diverse neuronal subtypes have also been identified using the single-cell RNAseq method.6 Thus, further investigation of single-neuron morphology and gene expression of the same single neurons could characterize the neuronal diversity more comprehensively. Finally, the functional relevance of the projectome subtypes revealed in this study is still unclear.

[source: Gao et al - 2022 - Single-neuron projectome of mouse prefrontal cortex.md] Discussion The organization of the neural network is likely to be designed for efficient signal processing under the constraint of the limited physical space available within the brain. Critical aspects of this organization include the appropriate strategic spatial distribution of neuronal somata, the arrangement of axons within the fiber tract, the collateral branch patterns relative to their target locations and the tiling of axon terminal arbors within the target areas to achieve wiring specificity as well as economy. In our study, we found that most projectome subtypes reside in selected areas rather than across all PFC areas. First-order axon collateral branch point location is correlated with axon target selection, and the spatial organization of terminal arbor domains of projectome subtypes demarcate the subdivisions of a target structure. It is worth noticing that our unbiased clustering method using FNT-dist based on whole-axon morphology yielded consistent but different results from those based on pre-defined targets, such as cortical subnetworks. It is still unclear which method serves as a better criterion for subtype classification. Furthermore, the functional importance of three distinct PFC modules with strong intra-module recurrent connectivity remains to be further examined. Finally, our finding of one-to-many relationship between transcriptome and projectome subtypes supports the notion that single-cell projectome analysis should be considered together with scRNA-seq analysis to refine PFC subtype definition.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Relationship between soma location, dendritic, and axon morphology The somatic and dendritic location of SPNs is important for determining sensory signal inputs, $^{1,5}$ and the central targets of their axonal projections likely depend on the sensory information they receive. However, the relationship between the soma location and the pattern of central axon targets of SPNs remains largely unclear. We found that soma and dendritic location of some projectome-defined SPNs subtypes exhibited strong preferences in specific areas or laminae of the dorsal spinal cord, although not for all subtypes. These data support that distinct projectome-defined SPNs subtypes could be differentially involved in transmitting various modalities of somatosensory formation. This is consistent with the fact that periphery sensory fibers processing different submodalities of somatosensory information terminate in different laninae. $^{1}$ We have also observed a correlation between axonal projection patterns and soma location for some thalamic relay neurons. An interesting question is whether a neuron achieve appropriate matching between dendritic inputs and axonal outputs, or vice versa. Our single-cell morphology reconstruction achieved a 3D view of the full morphology of SPNs. For the relationship between the total length of axon arbors and that of dendritic arbors, we revealed high correlation for 11 out of 19 projectome-defined SPN subtypes. Additionally, some projectome-defined subtypes exhibited obvious preference for specific dendritic patterns.

[source: Li et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectomes of mouse paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus oxytocin neurons reveal mutually exclusive projection patterns.md] Single-neuron reconstruction of axons, dendrites and somata Single cell axonal projections were manually reconstructed from three sparsely and brightly labeled samples, aided by the FNT software.[25] Full axonal arbors of 115 neurons from sample 18696 (lactating female), 65 neurons from sample 195037 (virgin female) and 84 neurons from sample 195038 (virgin female) were traced. To ensure accurate reconstruction, all axonal arbors were traced by two independent experienced tracers ( $>3$ months of tracing experience); reconstructed results were then merged and examined by another experienced tracer. A previous study, which used the same FNT software, examined tracing quality using quantitative measurements and showed that experienced tracers generated very similar reconstructions, and that accuracy was further increased by merging.[25] Tracing starting points were bright terminals outside of the PVH, to avoid bias in soma positioning; all brightly labeled neurons were traced. As shown in Videos S1 and S2, tracing was done using $0.35 \times 0.35 \times 1.0 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$ high resolution image datasets. The FNT software subdivided datasets into cubes ( $89.6 \times 89.6 \times 100 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$ ), and automatically loaded the next cube to be traced. At this resolution, axons can be easily distinguished from each other. Occasionally, when an axon tangled with another fiber near the soma, we traced both fibers and usually resolved the issue; occasionally, tracing was abandoned because axons could not be traced back to the soma.

The raw data was down-sampled to the resolution of $20 \times 20 \times 20\mu \mathrm{m}^3$ for the overview of the whole-brain data. FNT was used for reconstruction of the full morphology of neurons as described previously.[26,71] During tracing, the cube that users selected was loaded into the computer memory automatically and visualized in 3D by maximal intensity projection algorithm. FNT tracing process is semi-automatic: 1) a putative path can be found by A-star algorithm only with a starting position; 2) the human tracers will confirm and make revision manually. All neurons were reconstructed by two independent experienced tracers; then these two reconstructed results were merged and examined by another experienced person to obtain the final results. To quantitatively analyze data in the brain, we mapped our reconstructed neurons onto CCFv3. [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] SUMMARY The mammalian cortex orchestrates sensory processing, motor control, and cognition through a complex neural network, yet the organization principles governing single-neuron connectivity and its relationship with transcriptome and neuron activity remain elusive. Here, we reconstructed the projectomes of nearly 20,000 neurons in the whole mouse cortex, identifying 346 projection-defined subtypes with region- and layer-specific distributions. Our analysis uncovered seven cortico-cortical modules with submodular organization, high-resolution cortical hierarchy, and diverse terminal arborization patterns of single neurons refining the traditional feedforward/feedback model. Furthermore, we revealed cortico-subcortical projections, including multiple hyper-direct cortico-basal ganglia pathways, and constructed the detailed topographic maps between cortical neurons and their subcortical target regions. Finally, we showed that our fine-grained cortico-cortical connectivity map is closely related to the cortex-wide $\mathsf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ activity, electrical neuronal activity, and gene expression. Together, our multimodal analysis provides a foundational framework for understanding the cortical neural network in the mouse brain.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] The reconstruction of single-neuron projectomes in mammalian brains has advanced rapidly in recent years with the development of whole-brain imaging techniques7,8 and efficient pipelines of neurite tracing in large light-microscopy datasets.8–11 We previously reconstructed over 6,000 single-neuron projectomes in the mouse prefrontal cortex (PFC),10 from which we further mapped the fine-grained connectivity of the PFC by joint analysis of the morphology of single-neuron dendrites and axons.12 These studies showed that the unbiased mapping of singleneuron projectomes in the entire mouse cortex can facilitate a systematic understanding of the organization of the cortex. Moreover, multimodal analysis integrating single-neuron projectomes with the data of spatial transcriptomics, cortex-wide functional imaging, and large-scale in vivo electrophysiological recording is important to uncover the relationship between brain structure, gene expression, and functions.

retrieved_docs: [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] TB-sized CH1 images were processed into one million data cubes with $256 \times 256 \times 90$ voxels using the FNT-slice2cube program of the Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT) software.[26] Cubes used for projectome reconstruction were then compressed with the high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) method. The raw data was down-sampled to the resolution of $20 \times 20 \times 20\mu \mathrm{m}^3$ for the overview of the whole-brain data. FNT was used for reconstruction of the full morphology of neurons as described previously.[26,71] During tracing, the cube that users selected was loaded into the computer memory automatically and visualized in 3D by maximal intensity projection algorithm. FNT tracing process is semi-automatic: 1) a putative path can be found by A-star algorithm only with a starting position; 2) the human tracers will confirm and make revision manually. All neurons were reconstructed by two independent experienced tracers; then these two reconstructed results were merged and examined by another experienced person to obtain the final results. In our tracing process, only neurons with tracing score higher than 90 were included for further analysis. The neuron tracing score was calculated based on the protocols published previously.[26]

To ensure accurate reconstruction, all axonal arbors were traced by two independent experienced tracers ( $>3$ months of tracing experience); reconstructed results were then merged and examined by another experienced tracer. A previous study, which used the same FNT software, examined tracing quality using quantitative measurements and showed that experienced tracers generated very similar reconstructions, and that accuracy was further increased by merging.[25] Tracing starting points were bright terminals outside of the PVH, to avoid bias in soma positioning; all brightly labeled neurons were traced. The FNT software subdivided datasets into cubes ( $89.6 \times 89.6 \times 100 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$ ), and automatically loaded the next cube to be traced. Occasionally, when an axon tangled with another fiber near the soma, we traced both fibers and usually resolved the issue; occasionally, tracing was abandoned because axons could not be traced back to the soma.

Such single-neuron projectome analysis for PFC neurons, at a scale comparable to scRNA-seq, is required for a more comprehensive understanding of the diversity of neuron subtypes and the organization principle of their projectomes. However, whole-brain tracing of large numbers of single-neuron projectomes based on terabyte (TB) imaging data poses a formidable challenge. The PFC is the center of high-level cognitive functions, including decision-making $^{11,12}$ , working memory $^{13,14}$ , emotion $^{15,16}$ , attention $^{15,17}$ and perception $^{18,19}$ and is implicated in many neuropsychiatric diseases $^{20}$. Whole-brain connectivity based on bulk labeling of neuronal populations has shown that mouse PFC has extensive connections to nearly all brain areas $^{6}$. More precise long-range projection patterns of individual neurons will provide further functional specificity of diverse subtypes of PFC neurons $^{21,22}$. Although the hierarchical relationship between PFC and other cortical regions has been recently characterized $^{6}$ , the hierarchical ordering of subregions within PFC remains to be clarified. Thus, systematic characterization of PFC single-neuron projectome is critical for elucidating precise connectivity both within and outside PFC. In this study, we developed a software package, Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT), for high-throughput projectome reconstruction and analysis for TB-sized light microscopic imaging data.

The network analysis of such fine-grained cortico-cortical connectivity revealed seven cortico-cortical modules with further sub-modularity, such as the subdomains of visual areas involved in dorsal/ventral visual streams. The similar organization was also found in the visual areas of monkeys and humans.54 We found both similarities and differences between our modular organization of mouse cortex based on single-neuron projectomes and those reported in Zingg et al.3 and Harris et al.4 using bulking tracing methods. While we all identified the sensorimotor, visual, and auditory modules, lateral modules identified in Zingg et al.3 and Harris et al.4 were divided into two parts in our result, each assigned into adjacent modules. Namely, $\mathsf { A l d } / \mathsf { v }$ , gustatory areas (GU), and visceral area (VISC) belonged to sensorimotor module (MO/SS-1) in our result, while PERI, ectorhinal area (ECT), and TEa belonged to auditory modules. Such inconsistency may be caused by the dense connections among PERI, ECT, TEa, and AUDp/d/v (see Figures 2C–2E in Zingg et al.3 ).

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] Modular organization of the cortico-cortical connectivity network To unbiasedly investigate the cortico-cortical connectivity without predefined cortical regions, we spatially subdivided the entire cortex into a series of cortical ‘‘columns’’ $( n = 2 5 5 )$ ) with similar volume size $( 0 . 2 4 3 ~ \pm ~ 0 . 0 0 5 ~ \mathrm { { \ m m } } ^ { 3 }$ , mean $\pm$ SEM) (Figure 2A). The spatial resolution of cortical columns is much higher than that of the annotated cortical areas in Allen CCFv3 $( 1 . 4 3 3 \pm 0 . 2 1 3 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 }$ , mean $\pm$ SEM) (Figure 2A). Next, we quantified the cortico-cortical connectivity at the column level (Figures 2A and S5A). The cortico-cortical connectivity matrix is overall symmetric with the projection strengths of intercolumnar connectivity highly correlated $( 5 0 . 2 \%$ , $ { n } = \ 1 , 3 3 6 /$ 2,659), but we also found many asymmetric inter-columnar connections as shown in Figure S5B. Besides, the extent of input and output differs among cortical areas, with the motor area receiving the most axon inputs and sending the most axon outputs (Figure S5C).

These seven connectivity modules correspond to prefrontal, visual, auditory, anterior cingulate area (ACA)/retrospenial area (RSP), and three subregions in somatomotor areas (MO)/somatosensory areas (SS) (MO/SS-1/2/3). For example, three separate connectivity modules in somatosensory and motor areas were identified in our results, i.e., MO/SS-1/2/3, in line with the experimental results showing that the lateral part of the motor cortex (MO/SS-1), not the other parts of the motor cortex (MO/SS-2/3), is involved in mouse jaw movement.19 Furthermore, we found that the nodes of the prefrontal module showed significantly higher participation coefficients (Figure 2D; STAR Methods), indicating the unique role of the PFC in coordinating the whole-cortex connectivity network. We identified distinct groups of projectome subtypes projecting to each of the four cortico-cortical subnetworks. Interestingly, projectome analysis showed that the segregation of first-order axon collaterals can define different subnetworks. Further analysis also revealed that the somata of each subtype are distributed with specific topography within PFC; that the collateral branch location on the primary axon correlates with the proximity of the target; and that the distribution of axon terminal arbors at the target divides the target into subdomains. In addition, intra-PFC connectivity analysis based on projectome data allowed us to define a hierarchical order of PFC subregions and three distinct intra-PFC modules. Finally, the combined analysis of single-cell transcriptomes and projectomes showed that the same transcriptome subtype corresponds to multiple projectome subtypes found in different PFC subregions. Taken together, this work provides a comprehensive resource for mouse PFC projectomes at the single-neuron level and demonstrates how this resource could be used to reveal organizing principles of whole-brain PFC projections.
