Such single-neuron projectome analysis for PFC neurons, at a scale comparable to scRNA-seq, is required for a more comprehensive understanding of the diversity of neuron subtypes and the organization principle of their projectomes. However, whole-brain tracing of large numbers of single-neuron projectomes based on terabyte (TB) imaging data poses a formidable challenge. The PFC is the center of high-level cognitive functions, including decision-making $^{11,12}$ , working memory $^{13,14}$ , emotion $^{15,16}$ , attention $^{15,17}$ and perception $^{18,19}$ and is implicated in many neuropsychiatric diseases $^{20}$. Whole-brain connectivity based on bulk labeling of neuronal populations has shown that mouse PFC has extensive connections to nearly all brain areas $^{6}$. More precise long-range projection patterns of individual neurons will provide further functional specificity of diverse subtypes of PFC neurons $^{21,22}$. Although the hierarchical relationship between PFC and other cortical regions has been recently characterized $^{6}$ , the hierarchical ordering of subregions within PFC remains to be clarified. Thus, systematic characterization of PFC single-neuron projectome is critical for elucidating precise connectivity both within and outside PFC. In this study, we developed a software package, Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT), for high-throughput projectome reconstruction and analysis for TB-sized light microscopic imaging data.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] We calculated the dissimilarity matrix among all cortical neurons using FNT-dist (Figure 1D; STAR Methods). We found that the three top-level neuron classes (IT, PT, and CT neurons) were well separated (Figure 1D). Within the IT, PT, and CT neurons, the axon morphology is strongly dependent on soma locations across cortical areas and laminar depths (Figure 1E). Using hierarchical clustering, we identified 346 projectome-defined neuron subtypes consisting of 201 IT, 78 PT, and 67 CT subtypes (Figures 1F, 1G, and S2–S4; Table S2). The somata of these subtypes exhibited topographic distribution over the mouse cortex. In each of 43 cortical regions, there are multiple enriched projectome subtypes of IT, PT, and CT neurons (Table S3). As an example, we displayed representative projectome subtypes enriched in SSp-bfd (Figure 1H). Together, we generated a comprehensive dataset of single-neuron projectomes in the whole mouse cortex covering all major types of cortical projection neurons and obtained an unbiased classification of cortical projection neurons.

The morphologies of these major neuron types are generally consistent with previous reports (Figure S1E).1 Furthermore, we found that the neurons labeled by each Cre line are specifically enriched in morphology-defined neuron classes (Figure 1C), consistent with the previous classification of cortical glutamatergic neurons based on the transcriptome analysis.15,16 Notably, L6 IT neurons cannot be uniquely labeled by any mouse Cre lines4 but can be identified by their projectomes in our study.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] Limitations of the study There are several limitations in our study. First, our dataset is still limited in the number of reconstructed neurons, as it covers a small fraction of actual cortical projection neurons in the mouse brain. The current strategy of sparse sampling may obscure the rare subtypes. More sophisticated intersectional strategies could improve the coverage of projection neurons. Second, the reproducibility of these projectome subtypes of cortical neurons is an important issue. Our definition of neuron subtypes still needs to be cross-validated with other methods.46 Third, for cortico-subcortical projections, although we mapped the finegrained projections from the cortex, these subcortical targets also receive inputs from the brain regions other than cortex. For example, striatum also receives inputs from thalamus. Therefore, a complete description of neural network is still lacking. Fourth, our definition of neuron subtypes was based mostly on the neuron morphologies. However, diverse neuronal subtypes have also been identified using the single-cell RNAseq method.6 Thus, further investigation of single-neuron morphology and gene expression of the same single neurons could characterize the neuronal diversity more comprehensively. Finally, the functional relevance of the projectome subtypes revealed in this study is still unclear.

The network analysis of such fine-grained cortico-cortical connectivity revealed seven cortico-cortical modules with further sub-modularity, such as the subdomains of visual areas involved in dorsal/ventral visual streams. retrieved_docs: [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] SUMMARY The mammalian cortex orchestrates sensory processing, motor control, and cognition through a complex neural network, yet the organization principles governing single-neuron connectivity and its relationship with transcriptome and neuron activity remain elusive. Here, we reconstructed the projectomes of nearly 20,000 neurons in the whole mouse cortex, identifying 346 projection-defined subtypes with region- and layer-specific distributions. Our analysis uncovered seven cortico-cortical modules with submodular organization, high-resolution cortical hierarchy, and diverse terminal arborization patterns of single neurons refining the traditional feedforward/feedback model. Furthermore, we revealed cortico-subcortical projections, including multiple hyper-direct cortico-basal ganglia pathways, and constructed the detailed topographic maps between cortical neurons and their subcortical target regions. Finally, we showed that our fine-grained cortico-cortical connectivity map is closely related to the cortex-wide $\mathsf { C a } ^ { 2 + }$ activity, electrical neuronal activity, and gene expression. Together, our multimodal analysis provides a foundational framework for understanding the cortical neural network in the mouse brain.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] DISCUSSION This study presents the most comprehensive dataset of nearly 20,000 single-neuron projectomes in the mouse cortex. We provided a compendium of 346 neuron subtypes defined by projectomes. We found that the network of cortico-cortical connectivity is organized hierarchically with small-scale modular structures embedded within large-scale modular structures. We identified 12 laminar termination patterns of cortical arbors as the building blocks for constructing a high-resolution map of cortical hierarchy and unraveled the underappreciated heterogeneity of single-axon projections in FF and FB pathways of information transfer. Our in-depth analysis of cortical projections to basal ganglia revealed diverse joint projection patterns refining classical pathways and detailed projection topography defining fine-grained target subdivisions. Moreover, integrative analysis of structural connectivity, spatial transcriptomics, and functional activity data identified congruent gradients shared by both structural and functional connectivity networks as well as neuronal and molecular underpinnings of cortical hierarchy, advancing our understanding of how neuronal diversity may give rise to the complex cortical function. [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Definition of axonal trunk and terminal branches We defined a neuron tree hierarchy by assigning an order and depth for each axonal edge. The first axon edge from the soma is labeled as order 0, the following children edges with axon length longer than one-tenth of the maximum children edge and the bifurcation angle smaller than 45 degrees were labeled as parent's order, otherwise labeled as parent's order plus one. We repeated this process until all edges were labeled with an order. To determine the maximum depth of each edge, we set the terminal edge as depth 0 and the depth of its parent edge was defined according to its relationship with the children edges with maximum depth. If the order of parents edges was higher, then the depth of the parent edge plus one, otherwise similar with that of the children edges with maximum depth. We iterated this process for all edges. The axonal trunk was defined as the edges with the maximum depth greater than half of maximum depth of the entire neuron, or that with the maximum path from the branch point to all downstream terminal points is longer than one-tenth of the maximum path from root to all the terminals. Additionally, axon arbors were defined as the portion of edges that exclude the axonal trunk.

We found that the hierarchy score indeed showed significant correlations with many features of neuron spikes (Figures 7L and S12B). Among them, the neurons in low hierarchy tended to have shorter peak-to-trough duration of action potential, while those in high hierarchy tended to have higher peakto-trough duration (Figures 7M and 7N). This result is in line with the notion that the neurons in low-hierarchy areas respond more rapidly to the changing environmental sensory stimuli, whereas the neurons of high hierarchy take more time to integrate the information from multiple sources in sensory areas.53 Interestingly, we found that such correlation holds true among all neurons in superficial (L2/3 and L4) and deep (L5 and L6) layers (Figure 7L), indicating a universal organization rule throughout cortical layers and cortical regions. Among them, we found a negative correlation between the density of parvalbumin (PV) neurons and cortical hierarchy score (Figure 7H), in line with the previous studies.50 In addition, given that the ratio of PV and somatostatin (SST) neurons was suggested to be an indicator of cortical hierarchy,51 we examined the relationship between the ratio of PV neurons (052 Pvalb Gaba) to SST neurons (053 SST Gaba) and indeed found a negative correlation (Figure 7I). question: What advantage do single-neuron projectomes have over population-level viral tracing in whole-brain mapping?

question: What limitation does the sparse sampling strategy impose on the detection of cortical neuron subtypes?
retrieved_docs: [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] Limitations of the study There are several limitations in our study. First, our dataset is still limited in the number of reconstructed neurons, as it covers a small fraction of actual cortical projection neurons in the mouse brain. The current strategy of sparse sampling may obscure the rare subtypes. More sophisticated intersectional strategies could improve the coverage of projection neurons. Second, the reproducibility of these projectome subtypes of cortical neurons is an important issue. Our definition of neuron subtypes still needs to be cross-validated with other methods.46 Third, for cortico-subcortical projections, although we mapped the finegrained projections from the cortex, these subcortical targets also receive inputs from the brain regions other than cortex. For example, striatum also receives inputs from thalamus. Therefore, a complete description of neural network is still lacking. Fourth, our definition of neuron subtypes was based mostly on the neuron morphologies. However, diverse neuronal subtypes have also been identified using the single-cell RNAseq method.6 Thus, further investigation of single-neuron morphology and gene expression of the same single neurons could characterize the neuronal diversity more comprehensively. Finally, the functional relevance of the projectome subtypes revealed in this study is still unclear.

question: How did single-neuron reconstruction affect the traditional feedforward/feedback dichotomy?
retrieved_docs: [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] In the classical model of the trans-thalamic cortico-cortical circuit, CT neurons in low-order sensory areas (i.e., visual, auditory, and somatosensory areas) project to both first- and high-order thalamic nuclei, while PT neurons in these areas project only to high-order thalamic nuclei from which the information is FF to higher-order cortical areas.38 Here, we tested this model by examining the organization of cortico-thalamic projections at the single-neuron level. Interestingly, in contrast to the classical model, we found that both CT and PT neurons in VISp can project to either LGd (a first-order thalamic nuclei) only, or LP (a high-order thalamic nuclei) only, or both LGd and LP (Figures 5D and 5E). Thus, we proposed a revised model in Figure 5F, highlighting the fine-grained specificity at the singleneuron level. Similarly, we found that single PT neurons in auditory (Figures S11A and S11B) and somatosensory areas (Figures S11C and S11D) can also project to both first-order and higher-order thalamic nuclei, obeying the revised model of the CT circuit. Thus, single-neuron analysis of cortico-thalamic projections challenged the classical model and revealed a finegrained wiring diagram of the CT circuit for the low-order sensory cortical areas.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] Cortical hierarchy revealed by single-neuron projectomes Single-neuron reconstruction provided us the detailed information of axon termination patterns, refining the traditional FF/FB dichotomy. For instance, the separation of L1 and L6 targeting patterns challenges previous bulk-tracing models. While cortical hierarchy was defined for a population of neurons located in specific cortical regions, the violation of strict cortical hierarchical ordering can often occur at the single-neuron level, as we observed in VISp, VISa, and ACA. Li*, Haishan Yao*, Hui Gong*, Yan-Gang Sun*, Chun Xu* INTRODUCTION: In the brain circuitry, a single neuron could broadcast output signals to other neurons located in nearby or distant areas. Therefore, understanding the spatial organization of axon projections at the single-cell level is crucial for elucidating the neural circuitry underlying various brain functions. As a brain structure essential for learning, memory, cognition, stress responses and emotional behaviors, it is known that the hippocampus (HIP) is widely connected with various brain areas, including the cortex, thalamus, hypothalamus, olfactory areas, and amygdala. However, it remains unclear how single HIP neurons project to brain-wide target areas and how a single-neuron projectome can be specified by the soma location within the HIP. RATIONALE: To reconstruct single-neuron projectomes of the mouse HIP, we combined sparse-labeling methods with fluorescence micro-optical sectioning tomography and reconstructed the soma, axon arbors, and dendrites of individual neurons.

Further analysis also revealed that the somata of each subtype are distributed with specific topography within PFC; that the collateral branch location on the primary axon correlates with the proximity of the target; and that the distribution of axon terminal arbors at the target divides the target into subdomains. In addition, intra-PFC connectivity analysis based on projectome data allowed us to define a hierarchical order of PFC subregions and three distinct intra-PFC modules. Finally, the combined analysis of single-cell transcriptomes and projectomes showed that the same transcriptome subtype corresponds to multiple projectome subtypes found in different PFC subregions. Taken together, this work provides a comprehensive resource for mouse PFC projectomes at the single-neuron level and demonstrates how this resource could be used to reveal organizing principles of whole-brain PFC projections.

[source: Gao et al - 2022 - Single-neuron projectome of mouse prefrontal cortex.md] Discussion The organization of the neural network is likely to be designed for efficient signal processing under the constraint of the limited physical space available within the brain. Critical aspects of this organization include the appropriate strategic spatial distribution of neuronal somata, the arrangement of axons within the fiber tract, the collateral branch patterns relative to their target locations and the tiling of axon terminal arbors within the target areas to achieve wiring specificity as well as economy. In our study, we found that most projectome subtypes reside in selected areas rather than across all PFC areas. First-order axon collateral branch point location is correlated with axon target selection, and the spatial organization of terminal arbor domains of projectome subtypes demarcate the subdivisions of a target structure. It is worth noticing that our unbiased clustering method using FNT-dist based on whole-axon morphology yielded consistent but different results from those based on pre-defined targets, such as cortical subnetworks. It is still unclear which method serves as a better criterion for subtype classification. Furthermore, the functional importance of three distinct PFC modules with strong intra-module recurrent connectivity remains to be further examined. Finally, our finding of one-to-many relationship between transcriptome and projectome subtypes supports the notion that single-cell projectome analysis should be considered together with scRNA-seq analysis to refine PFC subtype definition.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] Limitations of the study There are several limitations in our study. First, our dataset is still limited in the number of reconstructed neurons, as it covers a small fraction of actual cortical projection neurons in the mouse brain. The current strategy of sparse sampling may obscure the rare subtypes. More sophisticated intersectional strategies could improve the coverage of projection neurons. Second, the reproducibility of these projectome subtypes of cortical neurons is an important issue. Our definition of neuron subtypes still needs to be cross-validated with other methods.46 Third, for cortico-subcortical projections, although we mapped the finegrained projections from the cortex, these subcortical targets also receive inputs from the brain regions other than cortex. For example, striatum also receives inputs from thalamus. Therefore, a complete description of neural network is still lacking. Fourth, our definition of neuron subtypes was based mostly on the neuron morphologies. However, diverse neuronal subtypes have also been identified using the single-cell RNAseq method.6 Thus, further investigation of single-neuron morphology and gene expression of the same single neurons could characterize the neuronal diversity more comprehensively. Finally, the functional relevance of the projectome subtypes revealed in this study is still unclear.

retrieved_docs: [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] DISCUSSION This study presents the most comprehensive dataset of nearly 20,000 single-neuron projectomes in the mouse cortex. We provided a compendium of 346 neuron subtypes defined by projectomes. We found that the network of cortico-cortical connectivity is organized hierarchically with small-scale modular structures embedded within large-scale modular structures. We identified 12 laminar termination patterns of cortical arbors as the building blocks for constructing a high-resolution map of cortical hierarchy and unraveled the underappreciated heterogeneity of single-axon projections in FF and FB pathways of information transfer. Our in-depth analysis of cortical projections to basal ganglia revealed diverse joint projection patterns refining classical pathways and detailed projection topography defining fine-grained target subdivisions. Moreover, integrative analysis of structural connectivity, spatial transcriptomics, and functional activity data identified congruent gradients shared by both structural and functional connectivity networks as well as neuronal and molecular underpinnings of cortical hierarchy, advancing our understanding of how neuronal diversity may give rise to the complex cortical function. The revealed principles—modularity, hierarchy, and subtype-specific wiring—provide a roadmap for investigating cortical computation and dysfunction in disease.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] High-resolution map of cortico-cortical connectivity A major advantage of single-neuron projectomes over the population-level viral tracing studies is the high spatial resolution achieved in the whole-brain mapping. The network analysis of such fine-grained cortico-cortical connectivity revealed seven cortico-cortical modules with further sub-modularity, such as the subdomains of visual areas involved in dorsal/ventral visual streams. The similar organization was also found in the visual areas of monkeys and humans.54 We found both similarities and differences between our modular organization of mouse cortex based on single-neuron projectomes and those reported in Zingg et al.3 and Harris et al.4 using bulking tracing methods. While we all identified the sensorimotor, visual, and auditory modules, lateral modules identified in Zingg et al.3 and Harris et al.4 were divided into two parts in our result, each assigned into adjacent modules. Namely, $\mathsf { A l d } / \mathsf { v }$ , gustatory areas (GU), and visceral area (VISC) belonged to sensorimotor module (MO/SS-1) in our result, while PERI, ectorhinal area (ECT), and TEa belonged to auditory modules. Such inconsistency may be caused by the dense connections among PERI, ECT, TEa, and AUDp/d/v (see Figures 2C–2E in Zingg et al.3 ).

For instance, the separation of L1 and L6 targeting patterns challenges previous bulk-tracing models. While cortical hierarchy was defined for a population of neurons located in specific cortical regions, the violation of strict cortical hierarchical ordering can often occur at the single-neuron level, as we observed in VISp, VISa, and ACA. [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] DISCUSSION This study presents the most comprehensive dataset of nearly 20,000 single-neuron projectomes in the mouse cortex. We provided a compendium of 346 neuron subtypes defined by projectomes. We found that the network of cortico-cortical connectivity is organized hierarchically with small-scale modular structures embedded within large-scale modular structures. We identified 12 laminar termination patterns of cortical arbors as the building blocks for constructing a high-resolution map of cortical hierarchy and unraveled the underappreciated heterogeneity of single-axon projections in FF and FB pathways of information transfer. Our in-depth analysis of cortical projections to basal ganglia revealed diverse joint projection patterns refining classical pathways and detailed projection topography defining fine-grained target subdivisions. Moreover, integrative analysis of structural connectivity, spatial transcriptomics, and functional activity data identified congruent gradients shared by both structural and functional connectivity networks as well as neuronal and molecular underpinnings of cortical hierarchy, advancing our understanding of how neuronal diversity may give rise to the complex cortical function. [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] SUMMARY The mammalian cortex orchestrates sensory processing, motor control, and cognition through a complex neural network, yet the organization principles governing single-neuron connectivity and its relationship with transcriptome and neuron activity remain elusive. Here, we reconstructed the projectomes of nearly 20,000 neurons in the whole mouse cortex, identifying 346 projection-defined subtypes with region- and layer-specific distributions. For example, we identified two submodules within the visual module (Figure 2F). Interestingly, the primary visual area, originally defined as a single cortical area in Allen CCFv3, is now divided into anterior and posterior parts, each belonging to a separate visual submodule. [source: Gao et al - 2022 - Single-neuron projectome of mouse prefrontal cortex.md] Discussion The organization of the neural network is likely to be designed for efficient signal processing under the constraint of the limited physical space available within the brain. Critical aspects of this organization include the appropriate strategic spatial distribution of neuronal somata, the arrangement of axons within the fiber tract, the collateral branch patterns relative to their target locations and the tiling of axon terminal arbors within the target areas to achieve wiring specificity as well as economy. In our study, we found that most projectome subtypes reside in selected areas rather than across all PFC areas. answer: Single-neuron projectomes refined the understanding of cortical submodules by revealing more detailed submodular organization within larger cortico-cortical modules and identifying distinct projection patterns. However, the functional importance of these submodules and the best method for subtype classification remain unknown.

We first chose a vertex on the surface of cortex as the anchor vertex, and calculated the geodesic distance between all other vertices on the surface of cortex and an anchor vertex. To project these vertices onto a 2D (U, V) coordinate system, we set the anchor vertex as the origin, the medial-lateral axis as the U axis, and the anterior-posterior axis as the V axis. The network analysis of such fine-grained cortico-cortical connectivity revealed seven cortico-cortical modules with further sub-modularity, such as the subdomains of visual areas involved in dorsal/ventral visual streams. The similar organization was also found in the visual areas of monkeys and humans.54 We found both similarities and differences between our modular organization of mouse cortex based on single-neuron projectomes and those reported in Zingg et al.3 and Harris et al.4 using bulking tracing methods. While we all identified the sensorimotor, visual, and auditory modules, lateral modules identified in Zingg et al.3 and Harris et al.4 were divided into two parts in our result, each assigned into adjacent modules. Namely, $\mathsf { A l d } / \mathsf { v }$ , gustatory areas (GU), and visceral area (VISC) belonged to sensorimotor module (MO/SS-1) in our result, while PERI, ectorhinal area (ECT), and TEa belonged to auditory modules. Such inconsistency may be caused by the dense connections among PERI, ECT, TEa, and AUDp/d/v (see Figures 2C–2E in Zingg et al.3 ).

retrieved_docs: [source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Region- and cortical-layer-specific targeting of thalamic relay neurons The thalamus is the major brain region for central relay of somatosensory signals.[29] We labeled thalamic relay neurons by injecting anterograde trans-synaptic virus AAV2/1-CMV-Cre[42] into the cervical spinal dorsal horn, followed by an injection of AAV-DIO-EYFP virus into the contralateral thalamus (Figure 3A), and reconstructed the full morphology of labeled neurons (Figures 3B-3D). These neurons distributed across many thalamic subregions, and their axons projected widely (Figures 3D, S9A, and S9B). The number of cortical areas innervated by neurons in higher-order thalamic nuclei was more than that by neurons in first-order thalamic nuclei (Figures S9C and S9D). We found that dendritic trees were relatively compact for most thalamic neurons (Figures S9E and S9F; Video S3), which could be important for relaying somatosensory information in a topographic manner. Then, employing the k-means method for clustering, we set $K = 50$ and partitioned the left SCm into 50 units of equal area. Subsequently, we propagated the labels of these voxel units along the direction perpendicular to the horizontal plane throughout the entire three-dimensional SCm, resulting in 50 columnar units in SCm. Next, we computed the axonal length from all spinal cord projecting single cells to each columnar unit, based on a standardized connection matrix $(ln(axon\ length + 1))$. Then we utilized hierarchical clustering to classify neurons using Euclidean distance and Ward's linkage.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] Compare our subdivisions with previous studies For the striatum, Hintiryan et al.30 identified 29 domains of dorsal striatum based on the bulk tracing of cortical inputs. Foster et al.29 further divided CPext.v into two parts (i.e., CPext.rv and CPext.cv) based on their differing input and output patterns. However, they conduct the quantification on 2D brain slices in Allen Reference Atlas (ARA)62 coordinate system while our subdivisions were computed in 3D in Allen ${ \tt C C F v 3 } ^ { 1 4 }$ coordinate system. Thus, we manually transformed the annotations of the 30 CP domains into the corresponding brain slices in Allen CCFv3. Then, we quantified the overlapping between the two annotations. For the SNr and GPe, Foster et al.29 identified 14 SNr subdivisions and 36 GPe subdivisions on 6 serial brain slices based on antegrade tracing in striatum. Similarly, since their study does not provide the annotation files in Allen CCFv3, we manually mapped their subdivisions to the corresponding brain slices in Allen CCFv3. Then, we quantified the extent of the matching between the subdivisions.

Then, these labels of patches were propagated to the whole cortex volume along the laminae direction based on the 'streamline' method.[26] The projection strengths in each cortical columns of all thalamic relay neurons were calculated instead of the analyses of the projection strengths in each brain region. Projection strengths in all columns constituted the projectome of each neuron. We applied hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distance and Ward's linkage, based on this connection matrix to identify neuron subtypes.

[source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] The organization of cortico-striatal projections has been extensively studied using bulk-tracing methods.30–32 Here, we examined the organization of cortico-striatal projection at the single-neuron level. We found that the axon terminals of IT neurons are of longer length and larger volume than those of PT neurons (Figures 4K and S9A). Using the same approach for the subdivision of SNr, we obtained 14 discrete striatal subdomains (Figures 4L and S9B; STAR Methods). Compared with the subdivisions of striatum previously identified by Hintiryan et al.30 and Foster et al.,29 we found that although the exact numbers of subdivisions were different ( $n = 3 0$ in Hintiryan et al.30 vs. $n = 1 4$ in this study), their spatial configurations were largely consistent (Figures S9C–S9E). Our topographic projection pattern was also similar to that in non-human primates,33 indicating a conserved feature of cortico-striatal projection. Moreover, we found highly consistent organizations of cortico-striatal projections for IT and PT neurons (Figures 4M, S9F, S9G, and S9H). Furthermore, we also observed convergent projections to striatal subdomains from different cortical areas. For example, striatal subdomain #11 receives convergent inputs from medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), AIv, and perirhinal area (PERI) (Figure 4N). Striatal subdomain #14 receives inputs from both ACA and subregions of visual areas (Figure 4O).

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] TB-sized CH1 images were processed into one million data cubes with $256 \times 256 \times 90$ voxels using the FNT-slice2cube program of the Fast Neurite Tracer (FNT) software.[26] Cubes used for projectome reconstruction were then compressed with the high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) method. The raw data was down-sampled to the resolution of $20 \times 20 \times 20\mu \mathrm{m}^3$ for the overview of the whole-brain data. FNT was used for reconstruction of the full morphology of neurons as described previously.[26,71] During tracing, the cube that users selected was loaded into the computer memory automatically and visualized in 3D by maximal intensity projection algorithm. FNT tracing process is semi-automatic: 1) a putative path can be found by A-star algorithm only with a starting position; 2) the human tracers will confirm and make revision manually. All neurons were reconstructed by two independent experienced tracers; then these two reconstructed results were merged and examined by another experienced person to obtain the final results. In our tracing process, only neurons with tracing score higher than 90 were included for further analysis. The neuron tracing score was calculated based on the protocols published previously.[26]

Occasionally, when an axon tangled with another fiber near the soma, we traced both fibers and usually resolved the issue; occasionally, tracing was abandoned because axons could not be traced back to the soma.
answer: The quality of single-neuron reconstructions was ensured by having two independent experienced tracers reconstruct each neuron, merging their results, and examining them with another experienced tracer. Only neurons with a tracing score higher than 90 were included for further analysis. Axonal morphology was simplified using farthest point sampling and FNT-decimate to preserve the global morphology of neurons, which facilitated the computation of dissimilarity matrices for clustering.

question: What manual landmark-based registration methods were used to align single-neuron reconstructions and to align top-view brain images with the Allen CCFv3?
retrieved_docs: [source: Gao et al - 2026 - Integrative analysis of single-neuron projectomes links connectome, transcriptome, and function in the mouse cortex.md] Image registration The image registration was conducted as previously described.10 To align single neurons reconstructed from different mouse samples, we manually segment several brain regions as landmarks and conduct image registration using Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs).59 The transformation parameters were then applied to the traced neurons to map them into the Allen CCFv3.

[source: Ding et al - 2025 - Single-neuron projectome reveals organization of somatosensory ascending pathways in the mouse brain.md] Registration of datasets to the template We developed registration strategies of our acquired brain-spinal cord datasets for various downstream analyses. To quantitatively analyze data in the brain, we mapped our reconstructed neurons onto CCFv3. The recognizable anatomical regions of the brain were chosen from the acquired image datasets and segmented as registration landmarks based on the cytoarchitectonic information provided by PI staining. Using Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs), we acquired transformation parameters by applying affine transformation and symmetric image normalization to the segmented landmarks.[28] These parameters were used for both neuron registration and high-resolution image registration. To quantitatively analyze data in the spinal cord, we mapped the reconstructed SPNs in the 3D spinal cord template. We marked as many dorsal roots from the acquired datasets as possible, although not all dorsal roots could be recognized. The outline and dorsal roots' coordinates of the spinal cord were served as landmarks during the nonlinear registration process. Briefly, we adjusted the posture of the dataset using the dorsal roots' coordinates of the template and dataset, and then nonlinearly transformed the dataset to the template, like brain registration strategy previously mentioned. Also, the unified template constructed in the previous part could also be regarded as an extended brain atlas, consisting of a brain image from CCFv3, and a brain-spinal cord image from the spinal cord template.

[source: Li et al - 2024 - Single-neuron projectomes of mouse paraventricular hypothalamic nucleus oxytocin neurons reveal mutually exclusive projection patterns.md] fMOST image registration to CCFv3 Features were extracted from the downsampled CH2 images at $10 \times 10 \times 10 \mu \mathrm{m}^3$ resolution for registration using Amira software. The selected features, as previously described, $^{88}$ include whole-brain outline, anterior commissure temporal limb (act), cerebellum outline, cc, CP, fasciculus retroflexus (fr), hippocampal region (HIP), MH, VIn, mammilothalamic tract (mtt), PVH, PG, VL, V3, AQ and V4. These extracting features were mapped to the equivalent structures in CCFv3 to obtain accurate transformation parameters. Following alignment of sample brains to CCFv3 in 3D, the SWC files of soma centers, and reconstructed axons and dendrites were warped to CCFv3 brain space using the generated deformation fields. To assess accuracy of registration, we overlaid the aligned boundary of CCFv3 brain structures to the downsampled CH2 images $(10\times 10\times 10\mu \mathrm{m}^3)$ (Figure S1). Registration was mostly accurate, except for some areas surrounding the ventricle system and in basal ventral brain regions; the ventricles in our samples were larger than those of CCFv3, making alignment of small nuclei below V3 difficult; adding more features did not improve registration accuracy. ME-projections of C1 neurons were most affected by this issue; the projection strengths and terminals of C1 neurons mistakenly registered to PVp were reclassified to ME, to more accurately reflect the true projection of these neurons. Other registrations were sufficiently accurate for subsequent analyses.

All mouse brain samples in this study were imaged by fMOST technology as previously described[24,25]. The fMOST raw image data contain two channels: EGFP channel (for neurite tracing) and PI-staining channel (for image registration). A typical EGFP channel consists of around 10,000 16-bit images in TIFF format of $30,000 \times 20,000$ pixels in size. The raw data are processed into 1,000,000 data cubes of $256 \times 256 \times 100$ voxels in size by the FNT-slice2cube command. The data cubes were then compressed with the high-efficiency video coding (HEVC) method. We also downsampled the raw data to the resolution of $20\mu \mathrm{m} \times 20\mu \mathrm{m} \times 20\mu \mathrm{m}$ for the overview of the whole-brain data. The manually labeled annotations and the interpolated annotations were stacked together to reconstruct the spinal atlas template in a three-dimensional space. After that, we manually marked a set of points representing the locations of 14 dorsal root of the cervical segment. For instance, the separation of L1 and L6 targeting patterns challenges previous bulk-tracing models. While cortical hierarchy was defined for a population of neurons located in specific cortical regions, the violation of strict cortical hierarchical ordering can often occur at the single-neuron level, as we observed in VISp, VISa, and ACA. question: How many LHA neurons were recorded during the single-unit recording across 7 mice walking on a linear track?
retrieved_docs: [source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] LHA glutamatergic neurons regulate motivation-driven locomotion To further understand how the firing rate of LHA neurons relates to locomotion speed, we performed single-unit recording at the caudal part of the LHA while mice were walking on a linear track. A total of 156 neurons were recorded from 7 mice. Figure 1I shows an example neuron with a positive correlation with the speed. Analysis revealed a correlation between the firing rate and the speed, using a speed filter previously described $^{7}$ , indicating that neuronal discharge relates to speed changes (Spearman correlation $P < 0.01$ ; $n = 37$ , median correlation 0.42) (Figure 1J). Subsequently, we applied two widely recognized criteria to categorize these neurons into putative principal cells, inferred to be glutamatergic neurons, and putative interneurons, believed to be GABAergic neurons $^{33,34}$. Out of these 37 neurons, we found that 24 exhibited characteristics of putative glutamatergic neurons, 3 exhibited characteristics of GABAergic neurons, and the remaining 10 were indistinguishable. (Figure S1F). Moreover, a subpopulation of neurons was found to increase their firing rate prior to the onset of locomotion (Figure 1K). The LHA is known to be critical for regulating various locomotion-dependent physiological and behavioral functions, including predatory attack, evasion, and other motivated behaviors $^{9,35,36}$. This functional diversity may arise from the heterogeneous cell populations and complex cytoarchitecture within the region.

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] LHA neurons regulate locomotion via projections to PnO and MSDB We next explored the circuit mechanism underlying the function of LHA projection in locomotion control. We searched in a single-neuron projectome dataset for mouse LHA for the major brain regions receiving axon projections from LHA neurons. This dataset consists of single-axon tracing of 916 sparsely labelled neurons expressing various neuropeptides (Figures S2A). To classify the pattern of axon projection patterns of these neurons, we calculated similarity scores based on the shortest distances between neuron pairs. We then performed hierarchical clustering of the similarity matrix of all neuron pairs using Ward's linkage. Using this approach, we categorized lateral hypothalamus neurons into 4 main clusters and 7 projectome-defined subtypes (Figures 2A-2B, and S2B), with subtypes 1 and 2 in the rostral projecting cluster (Cluster 1, $\sim$ $16\%$ of the total neurons), subtype 3 in the local projecting cluster (Cluster 2, $\sim$ $13\%$ of the total neurons), subtypes 4 and 5 in the caudal projecting cluster (Cluster 3, $\sim$ $46\%$ of the total neurons), and subtypes 6 and 7 in the long-distance projecting cluster (Cluster 4, $\sim$ $25\%$ of the total neurons). Among neurons grouped into subtypes 1 and 2 of the rostral projecting cluster (Cluster 1), most displayed targeting preferences for thalamus (TH) and cerebral nuclei (CNU), respectively. Notably, a distinct subgroup within Subtype 1 (TH-projecting) specifically projected to the lateral habenula (LHb).

A total of 156 neurons were recorded from 7 mice. Figure 1I shows an example neuron with a positive correlation with the speed. Analysis revealed a correlation between the firing rate and the speed, using a speed filter previously described $^{7}$ , indicating that neuronal discharge relates to speed changes (Spearman correlation $P < 0.01$ ; $n = 37$ , median correlation 0.42) (Figure 1J). Subsequently, we applied two widely recognized criteria to categorize these neurons into putative principal cells, inferred to be glutamatergic neurons, and putative interneurons, believed to be GABAergic neurons $^{33,34}$. Out of these 37 neurons, we found that 24 exhibited characteristics of putative glutamatergic neurons, 3 exhibited characteristics of GABAergic neurons, and the remaining 10 were indistinguishable. (Figure S1F). Moreover, a subpopulation of neurons was found to increase their firing rate prior to the onset of locomotion (Figure 1K). The LHA is known to be critical for regulating various locomotion-dependent physiological and behavioral functions, including predatory attack, evasion, and other motivated behaviors $^{9,35,36}$. This functional diversity may arise from the heterogeneous cell populations and complex cytoarchitecture within the region.

To investigate the association of excitatory versus inhibitory LHA neurons with motivation, we applied fiber photometry to record $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ signals of LHA neurons during food seeking. We injected AAV-DIO-GCaMP6s into the LHA of Vglut2-Cre or Vgat-Cre mice, allowing for the expression of GCaMP6s specifically in either excitatory or inhibitory LHA neurons, thereby facilitating fiber photometry imaging. We observed an increase of $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ signals of excitatory neurons that was time locked to the onset of locomotion, with elevated activity during food seeking behavior when approaching the food. However, these signals decreased during the consumption period (Figures 1L and 1M). LHA inhibitory neurons, on the other hand, did not respond to the onset of locomotion and food-seeking behavior; but increased their $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ activities during food consumption (Figures S1G and S1H). Meanwhile, in open field test, optical stimulation of LHA $Vgat^{+}$ cannot induce locomotion in freely-moving mice (Figure S1I). Next, to further explore the role of LHA $Vglut2^{+}$ neurons in basic locomotor function and motivated locomotion (e.g., food-seeking), we utilized AAV-DIO-DTR to selectively ablate these neurons.

We next aligned the axons of all PFC projection neurons and calculated the pairwise dissimilarity score of their axon morphology using a rigorous dynamic programming algorithm, FNT-dist (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Method 2). [source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] LHA neurons regulate locomotion via projections to PnO and MSDB We next explored the circuit mechanism underlying the function of LHA projection in locomotion control. We searched in a single-neuron projectome dataset for mouse LHA for the major brain regions receiving axon projections from LHA neurons. This dataset consists of single-axon tracing of 916 sparsely labelled neurons expressing various neuropeptides (Figures S2A). To classify the pattern of axon projection patterns of these neurons, we calculated similarity scores based on the shortest distances between neuron pairs. We then performed hierarchical clustering of the similarity matrix of all neuron pairs using Ward's linkage. Using this approach, we categorized lateral hypothalamus neurons into 4 main clusters and 7 projectome-defined subtypes (Figures 2A-2B, and S2B), with subtypes 1 and 2 in the rostral projecting cluster (Cluster 1, $\sim$ $16\%$ of the total neurons), subtype 3 in the local projecting cluster (Cluster 2, $\sim$ $13\%$ of the total neurons), subtypes 4 and 5 in the caudal projecting cluster (Cluster 3, $\sim$ $46\%$ of the total neurons), and subtypes 6 and 7 in the long-distance projecting cluster (Cluster 4, $\sim$ $25\%$ of the total neurons). Among neurons grouped into subtypes 1 and 2 of the rostral projecting cluster (Cluster 1), most displayed targeting preferences for thalamus (TH) and cerebral nuclei (CNU), respectively. Notably, a distinct subgroup within Subtype 1 (TH-projecting) specifically projected to the lateral habenula (LHb).

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] To visualize the hypothalamic areas that directly or indirectly projected to the hindlimb muscles, we first injected pseudorabies virus (PRV) encoding EGFP directly into the tibialis anterior/gastrocnemius (TA/GS) muscle. This allowed for retrograde trans-synaptic labeling of upstream neurons. The ClearMap $^{30,31}$ method was utilized for automatic analysis and registration of volumetric data from cleared tissues at 5 days after viral injection (see STAR Method). The reconstructed whole-brain data of labelled neurons were registered onto the standard Allen CCFv3 map, showing a widespread distribution of PRV-labeled neurons across the brain (Figure 1A). [source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] The LHA circuit in emotional valence processing The LHA's ability to integrate arousal, motivational and evasive underscores its role as a central hub for processing of emotional valence $^{10,53,54}$. Rather than functioning in isolation, the LHA is part of a broader network of brain regions that collectively shapes behavior in response to internal drives and external challenges $^{36,55}$ or primarily mediates appetitive locomotion $^{10,56-58}$. Our study demonstrated that LHA $Vglut2^{+}$ neurons projecting to the $\mathrm{PnO}$ play a crucial role in facilitating motivated locomotion, particularly during goal-directed behaviors like food-seeking. Importantly, locomotion was observed without the induction of anxiety or stress-like behaviors, indicating that the LHA-PnO circuit can selectively enhance motor functions associated with motivation without triggering negative emotional states. This finding is particularly interesting because it dissociates the locomotor and emotional functions of the LHA, which has traditionally been closely associated with both motor control and emotional regulation $^{36}$. While the LHA-PnO circuit facilitates motivated locomotion, a distinct projection pathway from the LHA to the MSDB appears to be involved in evasion and anxiety-like behaviors (Figures 3H and 3I). Neurons in the rostral LHA primarily project to subcortical (subtype 1) and thalamic areas, such as the lateral septum (LS) and lateral habenula (LHb), suggesting a key role for the LHA in emotional regulation, consistent with past research $^{59,60}$.

Two primary command centers in the brain, the subthalamic locomotor region (SLR) and the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), are responsible for transmitting locomotor commands to the central pattern generators in spinal cord $^{1-4}$. Extensively studies have revealed the role of MLR in controlling locomotion speed and various aspects of body movement $^{5-8}$ , but the mechanisms by which the SLR integrates internal/external stimulation and transmits locomotor commands to the spinal cord remain unclear. The lateral hypothalamus area (LHA) within the SLR has been implicated in motor control, particularly in motivated locomotion—internal need-driven movements such as food-seeking, exploration, or goal-directed behaviors $^{9,10}$. However, the precise LHA circuits controlling the locomotion, particularly within the contexts of motivation, remain incompletely understood $^{3,11}$. Recent single-neuron projectome studies have begun to reveal more detailed connections between specific neuronal subtypes in distinct brain regions, providing new insights into how these circuits may coordinate complex behaviors $^{12-16}$. Defining the neural circuits that control locomotion is also crucial for developing neural circuit-based strategies to promote motor recovery following injuries of the central nervous system (CNS).

The hypothalamus, located at the ventral base of the brain, is an evolutionarily conserved structure comprising numerous nuclei and interconnected neurons $^{1-4}$. It coordinately regulates neuroendocrine, autonomic and somatomotor responses crucial for maintaining vital behaviors and physiological balance. Hypothalamic control of behaviors and physiology relies on evolutionarily conserved neuropeptides $^{5,6}$. Despite their recognized importance, the axonal projections of hypothalamic peptidergic neurons remain incompletely understood. Previous studies used anterograde tracers such as Phaseolus vulgaris leucoagglutinin (PHL) to map projections from specific hypothalamic nuclei, revealing extensive brain-wide and intra-hypothalamic connections $^{7-14}$. Although informative, these studies could not distinguish projections of distinct peptidergic populations within the same nucleus. Recently, virus-mediated anterograde tracing has delineated projections of hypothalamic neurons expressing distinct neuropeptides $^{15-17}$ , but these bulk tracing methods could not reveal projections of individual neurons, particularly targets innervated by collaterals from the same axon. Notably, manipulating specific hypothalamic peptidergic populations often affects multiple behaviors and physiological processes $^{18,19}$ , suggesting their complexity and heterogeneity.

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] DISCUSSION The lateral hypothalamus, an evolutionarily conserved brain region, receives significant attention in the contexts of emotion, energy metabolism, and innate behaviors. Nonetheless, the elucidation of its function in the transmission of initiation commands to the spinal cord, as well as its prospective role in therapeutic interventions for disease, remains an area of ongoing investigation $^{46}$. In this study, we identified a population of glutamatergic neurons in the caudal LHA (cLHA) that transmit excitatory signals to pontine reticulospinal neurons in the $\mathrm{PnO}_2$ which in turn project to the spinal cord to initiate locomotion. We demonstrated that those $\mathrm{PnO}_2$ -projecting LHA $Vglut2^+$ neurons play a crucial role in motivated locomotion during food seeking behavior. Additionally, these neurons contribute to various aspects of motor recovery following incomplete spinal cord injury (SCI). Our findings underscore the importance of LHA circuits in transmitting locomotor commands to the spinal cord, advance our understanding of how supraspinal circuits facilitate functional recovery after SCI, and highlight a promising target for therapeutic interventions.

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] Brain-controlled LHA-DBS enhances locomotor recovery after sever SCI Previous findings have demonstrated that the delivery of DBS triggers stress responses in animals $^{27}$ and elevated stress levels were also observed under the condition of stochastic LHA-DBS despite stimulating specific locus at cLHA. To alleviate stress levels, we applied unsupervised learning algorithms to trigger LHA-DBS. The intention of locomotion can be decoded from the multi-unit activity (MUA) in the motor cortex's hindlimb region (M1HL) $^{27}$. Therefore, decoding this locomotor initiation information from the motor cortex could enable transient stimulation of the LHA via a brain-computer interface (BCI)-DBS system. To explore this, mice were outfitted with a 32-channel micro-wire array electrode implanted in M1 to record MUA and decode locomotor intentions. MUA firing rate increased prior to the initiation of hindlimb movements, observable in both intact and staggered SCI mice (Figures 6A and 6B). Under conditions of brain-controlled electrical stimulation, LHA-DBS did not provoke stress-like responses in either healthy or injured mice (Figures 6C-6F). These findings suggest that a BCI-DBS system could serve as a viable long-term therapeutic approach. To test this, staggered SCI mice underwent daily training sessions for 6 weeks, with brain-controlled DBS starting 4 weeks post-injury (Figure 6G). In contrast to the paralyzed control group, long-term BCI-DBS training resulted in significant functional recovery, including restored hindlimb stepping ability and increased BMS scores.

Second, the degree to which these findings can be translated to humans remains uncertain. Human spinal cord injuries are often more complex than the experimental models used in this study, involving a wider range of injury patterns, comorbidities, and longer recovery timelines. Further research is needed to determine whether similar mechanisms of motor recovery are applicable to human patients. [source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] DISCUSSION The lateral hypothalamus, an evolutionarily conserved brain region, receives significant attention in the contexts of emotion, energy metabolism, and innate behaviors. Nonetheless, the elucidation of its function in the transmission of initiation commands to the spinal cord, as well as its prospective role in therapeutic interventions for disease, remains an area of ongoing investigation $^{46}$. In this study, we identified a population of glutamatergic neurons in the caudal LHA (cLHA) that transmit excitatory signals to pontine reticulospinal neurons in the $\mathrm{PnO}_2$ which in turn project to the spinal cord to initiate locomotion. We demonstrated that those $\mathrm{PnO}_2$ -projecting LHA $Vglut2^+$ neurons play a crucial role in motivated locomotion during food seeking behavior. Additionally, these neurons contribute to various aspects of motor recovery following incomplete spinal cord injury (SCI). Our findings underscore the importance of LHA circuits in transmitting locomotor commands to the spinal cord, advance our understanding of how supraspinal circuits facilitate functional recovery after SCI, and highlight a promising target for therapeutic interventions.

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] INTRODUCTION Locomotion is a fundamental behavior essential for survival, enabling animals to seek food, evade threats, and engage in social and reproductive activities. Two primary command centers in the brain, the subthalamic locomotor region (SLR) and the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), are responsible for transmitting locomotor commands to the central pattern generators in spinal cord $^{1-4}$. Extensively studies have revealed the role of MLR in controlling locomotion speed and various aspects of body movement $^{5-8}$ , but the mechanisms by which the SLR integrates internal/external stimulation and transmits locomotor commands to the spinal cord remain unclear. The lateral hypothalamus area (LHA) within the SLR has been implicated in motor control, particularly in motivated locomotion—internal need-driven movements such as food-seeking, exploration, or goal-directed behaviors $^{9,10}$. However, the precise LHA circuits controlling the locomotion, particularly within the contexts of motivation, remain incompletely understood $^{3,11}$. Recent single-neuron projectome studies have begun to reveal more detailed connections between specific neuronal subtypes in distinct brain regions, providing new insights into how these circuits may coordinate complex behaviors $^{12-16}$. Defining the neural circuits that control locomotion is also crucial for developing neural circuit-based strategies to promote motor recovery following injuries of the central nervous system (CNS).

To alleviate stress levels, we applied unsupervised learning algorithms to trigger LHA-DBS. The intention of locomotion can be decoded from the multi-unit activity (MUA) in the motor cortex's hindlimb region (M1HL) $^{27}$. Therefore, decoding this locomotor initiation information from the motor cortex could enable transient stimulation of the LHA via a brain-computer interface (BCI)-DBS system. To explore this, mice were outfitted with a 32-channel micro-wire array electrode implanted in M1 to record MUA and decode locomotor intentions. MUA firing rate increased prior to the initiation of hindlimb movements, observable in both intact and staggered SCI mice (Figures 6A and 6B). Under conditions of brain-controlled electrical stimulation, LHA-DBS did not provoke stress-like responses in either healthy or injured mice (Figures 6C-6F). These findings suggest that a BCI-DBS system could serve as a viable long-term therapeutic approach. To test this, staggered SCI mice underwent daily training sessions for 6 weeks, with brain-controlled DBS starting 4 weeks post-injury (Figure 6G). In contrast to the paralyzed control group, long-term BCI-DBS training resulted in significant functional recovery, including restored hindlimb stepping ability and increased BMS scores.

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] LHA-PnO neurons facilitate motivation-related locomotion without inducing anxiety Next, we investigated the differential roles of MSDB-projecting and PnO-projecting LHA neurons in regulating mouse locomotion. Our findings demonstrated that optical stimulation of MSDB-projecting LHA neurons elicited high-speed running that resembled escape behavior, a response distinct from that observed following stimulation of LHA-PnO projections. (Figures 2J and 2K). Further open field test and elevated plus-maze test for the stress response of the mice indicated that stimulation of MSDB-projecting LHA neurons resulted in a significant reduction in the time at the center during the open field test and in the time in the open arms during the elevated plus-maze test. In contrast, stimulation of LHA-PnO axon terminals did not elicit any significant stress response (Figures 3A-3C). Through injecting retrogradely transported AAVs carrying Cre into the PnO while expressing Cre-dependent DTR in the LHA of wild-type mice, we found that depletion of PnO-projecting rather than MSDB-projecting LHA neuron terminals impaired motivation-related locomotion, as indicated by the reduced total distance and entries to the center compared to the control group (Figures 3D and 3E). Further examination of the soma distribution of neurons projecting to these two brain areas in single-neuron projectome data showed that somata for these two distinct projections exhibited a spatially distinct anterior-posterior arrangement (Figure 3F and S3A).

In conclusion, our study identifies the lateral hypothalamus (LHA) as a critical driver of locomotor initiation and recovery following spinal cord injury (SCI). [source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] These results guided us to apply LHA DBS in a specific location to facilitate functional recovery following severe SCI. Given the enhancement of locomotor recovery via activating the LHA-PnO descending pathway in lateral hemisection SCI mice, we questioned if similar manipulation could restore function in severe SCI models. Therefore, we employed a double lateral hemisection SCI model at T7 and T10 levels, creating a more challenging scenario by eliminating brain-derived innervation below the second injury site while maintaining a spared tissue bridge between lesions to relay descending signals $^{17,43}$. We conducted a timeline experiment to assess the effects of LHA-DBS on locomotor function, evaluating animals with and without LHA-DBS at post-injury weeks 1, 4, and 10, and analyzing immediate effects on hindlimb stepping (Figures 5L and 5M). Initially, no hindlimb responses were observed with LHA-DBS at 1 week post-injury. However, by 4 weeks after injury, animals exhibited significantly improved walking ability during LHA-DBS. Continuous DBS promoted pronounced locomotor improvements, as indicated by significant increases in maximum iliac crest height and stride length. 10 weeks post-injury, mice exhibited better locomotor functional recovery with LHA-DBS (Figures 5N-P). Subsequently, we aim to elucidate the mechanism by which LHA-DBS facilitates functional improvement in descending input-dependent movement.

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] Acute LHA electrical stimulation enables stepping in paralyzed mice after stagger SCI We next investigated whether more clinically relevant deep brain stimulation of the LHA could improve locomotion in mice with severe SCI. Our results indicated that stimulation of the LHA-MSDB pathway could induce significant anxiety-like behaviors (Figures 3H and 3I) that were detrimental to recovery. Therefore, we aimed to selectively stimulate the LHA-PnO pathway by adjusting the locus of stimulation within the LHA during DBS. Based on the somatic distribution of LHA neurons projecting to the $\mathrm{PnO}$ and MSDB, we identified that the cell bodies of LHA neurons projecting to the $\mathrm{PnO}$ are primarily located in the caudal region of the LHA (Figure 3L), whereas those projecting to the MSDB are predominantly situated in the rostral region. We injected AAVs carrying GCamp6s into both the $\mathrm{PnO}$ and MSDB and recorded the activation of these downstream brain regions during stimulation of different locations in the anterior-posterior axis of the LHA. Results showed that stimulating the anterior part of the LHA (-1.0 mm from the bregma) significantly activated the MSDB, while stimulation of the posterior LHA (-1.5 mm from the bregma) resulted in a higher amplitude activation of the $\mathrm{PnO}$ (Figures 5A-F). Moreover, electrical stimulation in caudal part within LHA induced locomotion immediately in intact mice (Figures 5G-K). These results guided us to apply LHA DBS in a specific location to facilitate functional recovery following severe SCI.

This is particularly important in the context of SCI, where emotional disturbances often can hinder the rehabilitation efforts to recover locomotion $^{64}$. # Therapeutic potential of DBS and its implications for clinical translation in SCI By elucidating the circuit mechanisms by which the LHA controls locomotion, we have expanded our understanding of using the DBS application to promote functional recovery after SCI. Our findings show that DBS stimulation of LHA, particularly targeting its glutamatergic neurons, significantly improved locomotor function in paralyzed mice. Guided by viral tracing and high-resolution fMOST analysis, we optimized the stimulation locus, primarily activating the LHA-PnO pathway rather than the LHA-MSDB pathway. This approach facilitated the restoration of locomotor function in SCI mice while minimizing the induction of stress. To maximize the efficacy of DBS, we further developed a brain-controlled DBS system that leverages real-time decoding of motor cortex activity to synchronize LHA stimulation with the intention to walk. This closed-loop system not only facilitated immediate improvements in motor function but also promoted long-term restoration of hindlimb motor function. By aligning LHA stimulation with the animal's intention to walk, this approach effectively harnesses the brain's natural drive to move, amplifying the effects of DBS and promoting more targeted rehabilitation.

This is particularly relevant in the case of SCI, in which the brain loses its direct connection with the SC. Despite neuronal death and axon degeneration after SCI, some axons and dormant relay pathways often remain spared across the lesion site, providing a neural substrate that can be reactivated to promote functional recovery, even with limited axon regeneration $^{17}$. The restoration of locomotor function after SCI involves the reorganization of both spinal and supraspinal circuits $^{18}$. Recent studies have unraveled brain region-specific contributions to motor function recovery after SCI, further arguing the importance of reactivation of the neural circuits involved in the regulation of locomotion control $^{19-22}$. However, effective therapeutic strategies for restoring motor function after SCI remain limited. As a promising strategy for in vivo neuronal activation, deep brain stimulation (DBS) offers the advantage of locally activating specific brain nuclei and has been successfully used to treat Parkinson's disease $^{23}$. Recent studies have also revealed that targeting specific MLR regions, including cuneiform nucleus $(\mathrm{CnF})$ $^{24-26}$ and pedunculopontine nucleus $(\mathrm{PPN})$ $^{27}$ , can enhance motor function and promote recovery in animal SCI models. However, the precise brain nuclei to target for optimal motor recovery remain under investigation $^{28}$ , and clinical trials are still in their early stages $^{29}$.

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] SUMMARY The hypothalamus is critical for regulating behaviors essential for survival and locomotion, but how it integrates internal needs and transmits locomotion commands to the spinal cord (SC) remains unclear. We found that glutamatergic neurons in lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) are essential for regulating motivated locomotor activity. Using single-neuron projectome analysis, trans-synaptic tracing, and optogenetic manipulation, we showed that LHA facilitates motivated locomotion during food seeking via pontine oral part (PnO) projection neurons, rather than direct SC projections or indirect stress signaling via medial septum and diagonal band. Activating PnO-SC projection neurons also initiated locomotion. Importantly, LHA-PnO projection neurons were crucial for regulating locomotor recovery following mouse spinal cord injury (SCI). Closed-loop deep brain stimulation (DBS) of LHA via gating by motor cortex signals markedly promoted long-term restoration of hindlimb motor functions after SCI. Thus, we have identified a hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway and the stimulation paradigm for potential therapeutic intervention after SCI.

The lateral hypothalamus area (LHA) within the SLR has been implicated in motor control, particularly in motivated locomotion—internal need-driven movements such as food-seeking, exploration, or goal-directed behaviors $^{9,10}$. Recent single-neuron projectome studies have begun to reveal more detailed connections between specific neuronal subtypes in distinct brain regions, providing new insights into how these circuits may coordinate complex behaviors $^{12-16}$. [source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] INTRODUCTION Locomotion is a fundamental behavior essential for survival, enabling animals to seek food, evade threats, and engage in social and reproductive activities. Two primary command centers in the brain, the subthalamic locomotor region (SLR) and the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), are responsible for transmitting locomotor commands to the central pattern generators in spinal cord $^{1-4}$. Extensively studies have revealed the role of MLR in controlling locomotion speed and various aspects of body movement $^{5-8}$ , but the mechanisms by which the SLR integrates internal/external stimulation and transmits locomotor commands to the spinal cord remain unclear. The lateral hypothalamus area (LHA) within the SLR has been implicated in motor control, particularly in motivated locomotion—internal need-driven movements such as food-seeking, exploration, or goal-directed behaviors $^{9,10}$. However, the precise LHA circuits controlling the locomotion, particularly within the contexts of motivation, remain incompletely understood $^{3,11}$. Recent single-neuron projectome studies have begun to reveal more detailed connections between specific neuronal subtypes in distinct brain regions, providing new insights into how these circuits may coordinate complex behaviors $^{12-16}$. Defining the neural circuits that control locomotion is also crucial for developing neural circuit-based strategies to promote motor recovery following injuries of the central nervous system (CNS).

In conclusion, it's noteworthy that we discovered an LH-PnO-SC excitatory circuit that can control locomotion without inducing negative emotional effects. LHA has extensive projections, the organization of which remains challenging to fully elucidate. In this study, high-resolution fMOST analysis classified its single-neuron projections into four major categories. Notably, a group of long-projecting neurons to the spinal cord, with approximately $48.99\%$ expressing orexin (FigureS3), was identified. However, activation of these direct spinal cord-projecting neurons in the LHA did not induce locomotion. In contrast, activation of neurons projecting to the PnO in the cLHA, including about $21.58\%$ orexin-positive neurons (Figure S5C), robustly initiated locomotion. The fMOST analysis also revealed intriguing projection patterns, including collateral projections to both the PnO and the PPN (Figure S3D), which play important roles in exploration. However, fewer neurons projected to the CnF, which is involved in escape behaviors. Taken together, these findings suggest that the LHA controls locomotion via pontine reticulospinal projections, functioning through an MLR-independent circuit, but potentially also through a PPN-dependent circuit. Other studies have also suggested that the PnO can transmit a variety of action commands, such as controlling locomotor gait asymmetries or inducing behavioral arrest $^{39,52}$.

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] SUMMARY The hypothalamus is critical for regulating behaviors essential for survival and locomotion, but how it integrates internal needs and transmits locomotion commands to the spinal cord (SC) remains unclear. We found that glutamatergic neurons in lateral hypothalamic area (LHA) are essential for regulating motivated locomotor activity. Using single-neuron projectome analysis, trans-synaptic tracing, and optogenetic manipulation, we showed that LHA facilitates motivated locomotion during food seeking via pontine oral part (PnO) projection neurons, rather than direct SC projections or indirect stress signaling via medial septum and diagonal band. Activating PnO-SC projection neurons also initiated locomotion. Importantly, LHA-PnO projection neurons were crucial for regulating locomotor recovery following mouse spinal cord injury (SCI). Closed-loop deep brain stimulation (DBS) of LHA via gating by motor cortex signals markedly promoted long-term restoration of hindlimb motor functions after SCI. Thus, we have identified a hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway and the stimulation paradigm for potential therapeutic intervention after SCI.

To explore the function of the LHA-spinal cord pathway, we expressed ChR2 in excitatory spinal cord-projecting LHA neurons by injecting retrogradely transported AAV-expressing Cre-dependent ChR2 into the spinal cord and implanting optical fibers in the LHA of Vglut2-Cre mice. This indicates that an indirect pathway from LHA to spinal cord might be involved. Based on our hierarchical clustering analysis, anterograde tracing and previous research in motor control $^{1,4-6,37,38}$ , we selected 3 potential downstream brain regions that receive projections from the rostral LHA neurons, including the LS, MSDB, and BST, as well as 7 downstream brain regions that receive projections from the caudal LHA neurons, including the substantia nigra reticular part (SNr), PB, LDT, PnO, PCG, gigantocellular reticular nucleus (Gi), and lateral paragigantocellular nucleus (LPGi), to determine their roles in locomotion (Figures 2G, 2H and S2C). [source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] DISCUSSION The lateral hypothalamus, an evolutionarily conserved brain region, receives significant attention in the contexts of emotion, energy metabolism, and innate behaviors. Nonetheless, the elucidation of its function in the transmission of initiation commands to the spinal cord, as well as its prospective role in therapeutic interventions for disease, remains an area of ongoing investigation $^{46}$. In this study, we identified a population of glutamatergic neurons in the caudal LHA (cLHA) that transmit excitatory signals to pontine reticulospinal neurons in the $\mathrm{PnO}_2$ which in turn project to the spinal cord to initiate locomotion. We demonstrated that those $\mathrm{PnO}_2$ -projecting LHA $Vglut2^+$ neurons play a crucial role in motivated locomotion during food seeking behavior. Additionally, these neurons contribute to various aspects of motor recovery following incomplete spinal cord injury (SCI). Our findings underscore the importance of LHA circuits in transmitting locomotor commands to the spinal cord, advance our understanding of how supraspinal circuits facilitate functional recovery after SCI, and highlight a promising target for therapeutic interventions.

[source: Ji et al - 2024 - Activation of hypothalamic-pontine-spinal pathway promotes locomotor initiation and functional recovery after spinal cord injury in mice.md] Functional reconstruction of the LHA in a model of spontaneous locomotor recovery following incomplete spinal cord injury Our results demonstrate that the LHA-PnO-Spinal cord descending circuits play a crucial role in facilitating motivated locomotion in intact mice, leading us to explore their potential involvement in voluntary locomotion following CNS trauma, such as SCI. We first characterized spontaneous locomotor recovery in mice received a lateral hemisection at the thoracic segment 10 (T10) $^{21,42}$. 3 days post injury, mice displayed a complete loss of stepping ability in the ipsilateral hindlimb, though muscle function in the contralateral hindlimb remained intact. In contrast, in the chronic phase post-SCI, we observed significant locomotor recovery in all subjects, characterized by full-body weight-bearing plantar stepping (Figures S4A and S4B). Next, we explored whether LHA neurons contribute to the observed recovery. To test this, we used two complementary sets of experiments (Figure 4A). Mice received PRV-labeling from the hindlimb muscle before injury, at the early (1 week post-injury) and chronic stage (8 weeks post-injury) after injury. Mice injected with PRV into GS/TA muscle at the early stage exhibited a marked reduction in neuronal labeling across the brain compared to intact mice, indicating disrupted descending pathways to the locomotor circuits below the lesion.
